attempts.answer:
Below is a practical, evidence-backed guide to finding patterns in breath data. Breath data broadly includes exhaled volatile organic compounds (VOCs) measured by GC–MS or portable micro-GC (breathomics), physiological respiratory signals such as airflow/flow–volume/pressure and respiratory sounds, and capnography (PETCO2 waveform). Patterns can be disease-specific signatures in VOC profiles, periodic/breath-cycle morphology and harmonics in airflow/sounds, transitions and irregularities (e.g., periodic breathing, hypoventilation, opioid-induced respiratory depression), and correlations with spirometry or clinical status. The approach below unifies preprocessing, segmentation, feature engineering, and modeling across these modalities, with disease-focused examples.

1) Start with a clear “pattern” hypothesis and modality plan
- Decide whether your “pattern” is compositional (VOCs) vs. temporal/structural (flow, sound, pressure, PETCO2), and whether you need within-breath events or breath-to-breath dynamics. Each modality has canonical features and pitfalls. For VOCs, patterns are multivariate chemical profiles; for flow/sound, they are morphological/asymmetric components and spectral energy; for capnograms, they are phase I/II/III morphology and PETCO2 trends. <cite id="5a5d82c9-0">Breathomics studies model exhaled VOC profiles as high-dimensional patterns linked to disease using supervised ML and SHAP to identify key VOCs</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-3">Across pulmonary diseases, ensemble models trained on hundreds of VOC features achieve high AUCs and specificity, with multicenter protocols linking VOC patterns to physiological metrics like DLCO</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-1">Respiratory sound/airflow pipelines emphasize denoising, time–frequency features, and dimensionality reduction to reveal signal patterns</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-1">Capnogram shape contains diagnostic patterns; automated extraction of physiologically grounded features enables COPD vs CHF and COPD vs normal discrimination with AUROC 0.89–0.98</cite>.

2) End-to-end workflow: preprocessing, segmentation, features, modeling, evaluation
- Capture clean data with modality-appropriate context: record sampling modality (bag vs endoscopic breath), device type (GC–MS, micro-GC, sensor arrays), and clinical metadata (disease labels, medications). For airflow/respiratory sounds, use electronic stethoscopes or flow sensors and log recording conditions; preprocessing must mitigate noise/artifacts and physiological overlap (e.g., heart sounds). <cite id="5a5d82c9-1">Breathomics pipelines require pre-processing including outlier exclusion, missing data imputation, and feature projection; decision-tree pipelines benefit from careful feature engineering and class balancing</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-1">Noise and heart sounds contaminate respiratory recordings; wavelet transform and empirical mode decomposition separate signal and noise while preserving morphology</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-2">Deep CNNs can learn directly from raw GC–MS chromatograms to detect VOCs automatically, outperforming expert-led analysis in speed and specificity</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-4">Deep learning spectrogram-CNNs and automated segmentation/time-labeling pipelines enable objective decomposition of breath sounds into intensities and frequencies for AI-based diagnosis</cite>.
- Segment breath cycles and events: detect inhale/exhale phases and locate abnormal components (creaks/rales/crackles or airflow irregularities). Practical detectors include zero-crossing and morphology-based rules; for sounds, EMD+Hilbert compute instantaneous frequency/envelope to find segments with abnormal dispersion; for flow, quartile-based labeling of inspiratory vs expiratory ranges supports within-breath analysis. <cite id="8a8be054-0">Time-domain features like mean amplitude, variance, RMS, peak-to-peak, and zero-crossing capture breathing irregularities for airflow pattern analysis</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-3">Zero-crossing–based segmentation of respiratory phases enables flow quartile assignment; Hilbert-spectrum–based detection of crackles/rales segments within breaths supports event-localized analysis</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-2">Wavelets capture multiscale irregularities but yield energy distributions; EMD-based decompositions isolate oscillatory components yet vary across realizations, complicating cross-subject interpretation</cite>.
- Feature engineering tailored to patterns:
  • Breathomics: peak intensities/areas of VOCs, ratio features, baseline correction and drift normalization; use tree-ensemble feature importance/SHAP to interpret which VOCs define disease patterns. <cite id="5a5d82c9-0">Ensemble models (XGBoost, RF/SVM) on public GC–MS breath datasets deliver strong classification; SHAP highlights key VOCs, reinforcing biological plausibility</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-4">Feature selection identifies disease-specific VOC sets (e.g., 9 markers COPD vs healthy, 5 markers asthma vs healthy), enabling high-performing RF/SVC/logistic models</cite>.
  • Airflow/respiratory sounds: time/frequency descriptors, spectral peaks, MFCCs; energy-based features; morphological asymmetry and skewness; wavelet coefficients; entropy measures for irregularity. <cite id="8a8be054-1">FFT extracts dominant frequency peaks; STFT and MFCCs provide time–frequency representations for nonstationary respiratory sounds; PCA/ICA reduce dimensionality while retaining structure</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-2">Wavelet-based features capture irregularities and asymmetries across scales, supporting classification when combined with oximetry/pressure</cite>.
  • Capnography: compute phase boundary locations, slopes/angles of phase III, PETCO2 end-tidal values, slope steepness, rise time, and shape descriptors; engineered ratios and derivatives can capture obstructive vs restrictive patterns. <cite id="04d9653a-0">Volumetric capnography waveform features (slope/angle, peak values) correlate with FEV1/FVC and differentiate obstructive vs restrictive disease; end-to-end AI or transformed capnograms can standardize and improve accuracy</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-1">Four physiologically grounded capnogram features enable discrimination of COPD vs CHF (AUROC 0.89) and COPD vs normal (AUROC 0.98) with fast runtime</cite>.
- Modeling choices:
  • For tabular breathomics profiles: gradient-boosted trees, RF, SVM; add SHAP/feature attribution to validate disease-specific patterns. <cite id="5a5d82c9-0">Across seven classifiers, ensembles (XGBoost) achieved strong performance; SHAP-based interpretability identified key VOC drivers of disease-specific predictions</cite>.
  • For capnograms: hand-crafted shape features with classical classifiers (QDA) or end-to-end CNNs; multi-stage time-series classifiers to handle rare abnormal events. <cite id="04d9653a-1">Physiology-informed features plus QDA ensembles achieve high AUROC in COPD/CHF vs COPD/normal classification</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-2">A multi-stage time-series classification approach separates normal vs abnormal patterns first to tackle class imbalance, then applies more complex models to the abnormal cohort</cite>.
  • For airflow/respiratory sounds: CNNs on spectrograms, MFCCs, or learned embeddings; hybrid models with oximetry/pressure; tree ensembles on engineered features; consider complex network/graph features for bronchial sounds. <cite id="8a8be054-4">Deep CNNs operating on spectrograms automatically recognize disease/abnormal lung sounds; automated segmentation extracts intensity/frequency parameters</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-1">Time–frequency features (STFT/MFCC) and dimensionality reduction (PCA/ICA) improve classification of respiratory sounds</cite>.
- Evaluation and robustness:
  • Report per-breath and per-subject metrics; cross-visit and cross-center validation; stratify by sampling modality and device generation (bag vs endobronchial sampling can change accuracy/bias). <cite id="5a5d82c9-1">Endoscopic breath sampling outperformed bag breath sampling in histology subtype classification and achieved 75% accuracy, underscoring sampling-method effects</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-3">Multi-center TD-GC×GC-HRMS protocols achieved high performance (AUC 0.82, 77% sens, 100% spec) and linked VOC markers to DLCO</cite>.
  • Address class imbalance and noise explicitly for anomaly detection (e.g., respiratory depression). <cite id="04d9653a-2">Opioid-induced respiratory depression is rare; multi-stage time-series classification mitigates imbalance by first separating normal vs abnormal patterns, improving anomaly detection efficiency</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-1">Variations in recording conditions and overlapping heart sounds require denoising and segmentation to avoid performance degradation</cite>.
  • For breathomics, include metabolite ratio features and background drift normalization; use imputation and outlier removal; validate model generalization across GC–MS platforms. <cite id="5a5d82c9-1">Pre-processing (outlier exclusion, missing data imputation, feature projection, and class balance) is indispensable; decision-tree pipelines improved with feature selection and balancing</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-2">Deep learning on raw GC–MS chromatograms bypasses subjective expert steps and increases consistency and throughput</cite>.

3) Pattern-finding by modality: concrete techniques and examples
- Breathomics (VOCs): 
  • Patterns: differential abundance of lipid peroxidation products, aldehydes, alkanes; VOC clusters aligning with disease pathways. <cite id="5a5d82c9-0">Interpretable ML on GC–MS breath VOCs identified key VOCs driving asthma/bronchiectasis/COPD predictions, enabling candidate biomarker discovery</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-3">In PTB, ensemble models on ~800 HRMS features achieved AUC 0.975 with high specificity; ILD classification identified nine VOCs with AUC 0.82 and 100% specificity</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-4">In a 367-patient cross-sectional study, nine VOCs separated COPD from healthy, and five VOCs asthma vs healthy; RF best discriminated COPD vs healthy (AUC 0.92)</cite>.
  • Practical steps: align chromatograms, extract m/z peaks and areas; normalize to breath depth/time and background blanks; select features via mutual information/recursive feature elimination or permutation importance; use ensembles with SHAP. <cite id="5a5d82c9-2">Deep CNNs learned to detect VOCs directly from raw chromatograms, detecting more VOCs faster with high specificity than expert-driven workflows</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-0">SHAP-based interpretability tied specific VOCs to predictions, supporting clinical translation</cite>.
- Respiratory airflow and sounds:
  • Patterns: amplitude variability, energy shifts, spectral peak emergence, crackle/rale bursts, asymmetric expiratory flow limitation, and periodic breathing. <cite id="8a8be054-0">Mean amplitude, variance, RMS, peak-to-peak, and zero-crossing rate distinguish normal from hypoventilation and characterize periodic breathing</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-1">FFT yields dominant frequency peaks; STFT/MFCCs capture nonstationary bursts, and PCA/ICA condense structure for ML</cite> <cite id="8a8be54-3">Hilbert-based instantaneous frequency/envelope analysis identifies crackles/rales segments, enabling time-localized classification</cite>.
  • Practical steps: denoise with wavelets/EMD; segment breaths via zero crossings and flow thresholds; compute spectral features and entropy; build RF/XGBoost or CNNs on spectrograms; for bronchodilator response, analyze flow quartiles per phase. <cite id="8a8be054-1">Wavelet/EMD denoising and feature extraction improve classification of normal vs adventitious sounds</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-3">Zero-crossing segmentation plus Hilbert-spectrum–based detection/classification of crackles/rales supports within-breath analysis tied to bronchodilator response</cite>.
- Capnography (PETCO2 waveform):
  • Patterns: phase III alveolar plateau slope (Slopes A–D), diffusion/dispersion artifacts, rebreathing loops, PETCO2 trends reflecting hypoventilation or shunting, and distinct shapes in COPD vs CHF vs normal. <cite id="04d9653a-0">Capnogram morphological features like slope/angle and peak values correlate with FEV1/FVC and help differentiate obstructive and restrictive lung diseases</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-1">Four physiologically based features plus QDA ensembles achieved AUROC 0.89 (COPD/CHF) and 0.98 (COPD/normal)</cite>.
  • Practical steps: detect phase boundaries; compute PETCO2 end-tidal and phase III slope; apply Hjorth activity and MAD to classify artefact-free vs distorted segments; use time–domain features with fast SVMs for real-time filtering. <cite id="04d9653a-3">Hjorth activity and mean absolute deviation features with polynomial-kernel SVMs achieved 89% accuracy/92.1% precision/91% specificity in artefact classification, with 13 ms per segment processing</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-4">Automated artefact-free vs distorted segment classification is essential before disease modeling and can be implemented for real-time capnogram assessment</cite>.
  • Anomaly detection: multi-stage TSC to detect opioid-induced respiratory depression by learning normal baseline dynamics, gating on movement/sensor health, and using synthetic minority oversampling or weighted losses; monitor false-positive rates. <cite id="04d9653a-2">Multi-stage time-series classification addresses class imbalance and recognizes relevant patterns in continuous capnography/SpO2, enabling faster anomaly detection</cite>.

4) Advanced modeling and anomaly/outlier detection
- Deep learning for temporal patterns: CNNs on spectrograms of airflow/sounds learn morphological invariants; RNN/LSTM/Transformer variants capture long-range breath-to-breath dependencies and transitions; end-to-end models on volumetric capnography can replace hand-crafted features. <cite id="8a8be054-4">Spectrogram CNNs end-to-end detect respiratory disease and abnormal sounds, supported by automated segmentation of time labels</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-0">Transformed volumetric capnography integrated with AI improves standardization and accuracy for diagnosis</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-1">End-to-end models inputting raw capnograms differentiated COPD-normal and COPD-CHF</cite>.
- Anomaly/outlier detection: density-based clustering (e.g., DBSCAN) on feature embeddings; autoencoders to reconstruct normal breath patterns and flag high-reconstruction-error segments; multi-stage pipelines separate normal vs abnormal first to reduce imbalance impact. <cite id="04d9653a-2">Multi-stage TSC with an initial separator of normal vs abnormal improves class imbalance handling and accuracy in anomaly detection for continuous capnography and SpO2</cite>.
- Interpretable pattern discovery: SHAP/feature attribution for breathomics; Hilbert IF/IE dispersion for identifying crackle/rale bursts in sounds; global shape descriptors in capnograms (phase III slope) map to physiology (airway calibre, alveolar diffusion). <cite id="5a5d82c9-0">SHAP identifies VOCs driving predictions in breathomics, enabling candidate marker discovery</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-3">Lower IF dispersion marks crackle/rale segments, providing interpretable criteria for abnormal component detection</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-0">Phase III slope/angle and peak features translate to spirometric indices (FEV1/FVC) and disease categories</cite>.

5) Validation, drift, and deployment considerations
- Internal vs external validation: stratify by site/device/disease stage; use blinded sets for capnography/breathomics to confirm generalization; ensure sampling modality consistency in breathomics. <cite id="5a5d82c9-3">Evaluations across validation and blinded test sets achieved AUC 0.975 and 92.6% accuracy for TB, demonstrating robustness and scalability of breath-based ML models</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-1">Sampling modality affects performance (EBS > BBS in one study), and careful feature selection and class balancing are critical</cite>.
- Drift and artifacts: implement runtime artifact rejection (motion/leak detection) and reference-channel gating; for breathomics, baseline correction and blank-subtraction; capnogram pipelines classify artefact-free vs distorted segments before analytics. <cite id="8a8be054-1">EMD/wavelet denoising and segmentation improve robustness to noise and interference in respiratory signals</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-3">Real-time artefact classification with simple time-domain features enables automated capnogram assessment</cite>.
- Clinical translation: link pattern features to physiology (e.g., VOC markers to DLCO; capnogram slope to FEV1) and provide decision support with explainability; track sensitivity/specificity and clinically meaningful effect sizes, not only accuracy. <cite id="5a5d82c9-3">ILD studies linked discriminative VOCs to DLCO and demonstrated multicentric protocols, reinforcing physiological relevance</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-1">Physiology-grounded capnogram features yield clinically actionable discrimination with high AUROC and fast runtimes</cite>.

6) A practical step-by-step recipe (choose your modality)
- Step 1: Record and log metadata
  • For VOCs: capture GC–MS or micro-GC runs with breath type (bag vs EBS), duration, tidal volume/flow, room background blanks, and clinical labels. <cite id="5a5d82c9-1">Sampling method and preprocessing critically affect performance; endobronchial sampling outperformed bag sampling in subtype classification</cite>.
  • For airflow/sounds: record flow/pressure and/or stereo/omni acoustic sensors synchronized with oximetry; note ambient noise, patient position, and medication. <cite id="8a8be054-1">Environmental noise and heart sounds require denoising before classification</cite>.
  • For capnography: collect continuous PETCO2 with SpO2; log ventilator settings, coughs/locomotion events, and device calibration times. <cite id="04d9653a-2">Continuous monitoring is affected by movement/calibration; ML must interpret long streams and handle imbalance</cite>.
- Step 2: Preprocess to extract patterns
  • Breathomics: align chromatograms; remove outliers and blanks; normalize per breath; correct baseline drift. <cite id="5a5d82c9-2">Deep learning directly on raw chromatograms bypasses subjective expert processing, increasing speed and specificity</cite>.
  • Airflow/sounds: denoise with wavelet/EMD; segment breaths via zero-crossing/flow thresholds; compute time/frequency features and entropy; for sounds, compute IF/IE and dispersion to localize abnormal components. <cite id="8a8be054-1">Wavelet/EMD preserve morphology while separating noise; FFT/STFT/MFCCs yield spectral features</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-3">Hilbert-spectrum–based detection of crackles/rales segments supports event localization</cite>.
  • Capnography: detect phases; compute PETCO2 end-tidal and phase III slope; classify artefact-free vs distorted segments using simple features for real-time filtering. <cite id="04d9653a-1">Physiologically based features enable fast, accurate discrimination between COPD/CHF and COPD/normal</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-3">Hjorth activity and MAD with SVM provide fast artefact classification (13 ms per segment)</cite>.
- Step 3: Feature selection and model choice
  • Breathomics: select VOC peaks and ratios; use tree ensembles with SHAP; consider deep CNNs on chromatogram tiles. <cite id="5a5d82c9-0">Ensemble models and SHAP identify key VOCs for asthma/COPD/bronchiectasis</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-2">CNNs on raw GC–MS detect more VOCs reliably than expert analysis</cite>.
  • Airflow/sounds: combine time/frequency features and morphology-derived statistics; train RF/XGBoost or CNNs on spectrograms; for bronchodilator response, stratify by flow quartiles. <cite id="8a8be054-1">Time–frequency features and dimensionality reduction improve classification of adventitious vs normal sounds</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-3">Flow quartile segmentation enables within-breath assessment of bronchodilator response</cite>.
  • Capnography: engineer phase/slope/shape features; train QDA ensembles or CNNs; deploy artefact classifiers first to reduce imbalance. <cite id="04d9653a-1">Four capnogram features with QDA ensembles yield AUROC 0.89–0.98</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-2">Multi-stage TSC improves anomaly detection under class imbalance</cite>.
- Step 4: Evaluate and iterate
  • Use cross-subject, cross-site, and blinded cohorts; report sensitivity/specificity and clinically interpretable effect sizes; retrain on new sensor generations/sampling modalities. <cite id="5a5d82c9-3">Blinded tests with ensemble models achieved AUC 0.975 and 92.6% accuracy for TB, with multicenter feasibility</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-1">Sampling modality influences performance, requiring external validation and feature engineering</cite>.
- Step 5: Deploy and monitor
  • Add runtime artifact rejection, drift detection, and explainability (SHAP for breathomics, IF/IE thresholds for sounds, shape/slope flags for capnography); set actionable thresholds and audit false alarms. <cite id="04d9653a-3">Real-time artefact classification enables automated capnogram-based assessment</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-0">SHAP-based interpretability reinforces model outputs and suggests biochemical markers</cite>.

7) Disease-focused pointers to recognizable patterns
- Asthma vs COPD and PRISm: breathomics models consistently separate these groups using VOC markers; airflow/respiratory sound analyses show increased high-frequency energy and crackle prevalence in small-airway disease. <cite id="5a5d82c9-3">VOC-based models (RF/XGBoost) on micro-GC data identified specific VOCs for COPD vs asthma and PRISm vs healthy, with high accuracies across disease pairs</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-1">Spectral energy and morphology features differentiate adventitious from normal lung sounds, supporting small-airway disease detection</cite>.
- Interstitial lung disease (ILD) and pulmonary hypertension: breathomics markers correlate with DLCO; capnogram patterns reflect diffusion impairment and right-heart involvement. <cite id="5a5d82c9-3">TD-GC×GC-HRMS models identified nine VOCs with AUC 0.82, 77% sensitivity, and 100% specificity, linked to DLCO</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-0">Capnogram features such as phase III slope/angle correlate with FEV1/FVC and differentiate obstructive vs restrictive disease</cite>.
- Opioid-induced respiratory depression: continuous monitoring pipelines detect deviations from normal cycle morphology and PETCO2 dynamics; multi-stage anomaly detectors reduce false alarms. <cite id="04d9653a-2">Imbalanced data and irregularities require multi-stage time-series classification; runtime is suitable for real-time monitoring</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-0">Zero-crossing and energy-based features capture hypoventilation and periodic irregularities</cite>.
- Tuberculosis and other infections: ensemble models trained on high-throughput mass spec profiles deliver high AUROC and accuracy; multicenter validation supports scalability. <cite id="5a5d82c9-3">For PTB (N=518 PTB, 887 controls), ensemble models achieved AUC 0.975 and 92.6% accuracy with high specificity</cite>.

Summary: To find patterns in breath data, align preprocessing to your modality’s noise and physiological overlap, segment breath cycles and events, engineer features that capture the hypothesized pattern (VOC composition, airflow/sound morphology, capnogram shape/dynamics), and model with tree ensembles (with SHAP/attribute masks) or deep CNNs on spectrograms/chromatograms; validate across sites/devices and clinical cohorts, and add runtime artifact/reconstruction-error monitoring for anomalies. <cite id="5a5d82c9-0">Interpretable ML on breath VOCs reveals disease-linked chemical patterns and supports clinical plausibility</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-1">Respiratory sound/airflow pipelines use denoising and time–frequency features to expose pathological patterns</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-1">Capnogram shape features and ensembles detect clinically relevant differences with high AUROC</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-2">Deep learning on raw breath-chemistry traces automates biomarker detection faster and more consistently than expert pipelines</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-2">Anomaly detection for respiratory depression benefits from multi-stage time-series classification to handle rare events and noise</cite>.

Limitations and next steps: Breathomics performance varies with sampling modality and platform; airflow/sound analyses can be confounded by recording conditions and heart sounds; capnogram interpretation requires robust artefact rejection. Address these by including modality/ device as covariates, deploying automated artefact filters, and conducting multi-center blinded validation. Emerging directions include learning breath-specific transformers and self-supervised embeddings across modalities, and integrating multimodal streams (flow + sound + PETCO2 + VOCs) for ensemble pattern discovery. <cite id="5a5d82c9-1">Sampling method (EBS vs BBS) affects classification accuracy and should be standardized or included in models</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-1">Variations in recording conditions and overlapping sounds necessitate denoising and segmentation for robust classification</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-3">Physiology-linked VOC markers and multi-center protocols show feasibility, but external validation remains essential</cite>.

Title: A baseline study of interpretable machine learning using GC-MS breath VOCs for classifying asthma, bronchiectasis, and COPD
Snippet: We present a reproducible, interpretable machine learning baseline for classifying asthma, bronchiectasis, and COPD from a public GC-MS dataset of exhaled breath VOCs. Across seven supervised classifiers, particularly ensemble-based models such as XGBoost, we observed strong diagnostic performance across multiple evaluation metrics. The incorporation of SHAP-based interpretability further enabled the identification of key VOCs driving disease-specific predictions, providing candidate biochemical markers and reinforcing the biological plausibility of model outputs. These results underscore the utility of breathomics not only as a practical diagnostic alternative to invasive or subjective diagnostic tools but also as a pathway toward transparent and explainable respiratory disease classification. By establishing this reproducible and interpretable baseline, our work provides a reference point for future methodological advancements and external validation in breathomics-based diagnostics.
</snippet>

Title: Exploratory study on classification of lung cancer subtypes through a combined K-nearest neighbor classifier in breathomics
Snippet: problem of lung cancer subtypes in vitro 15 . In 2012, Barash et al. proved that combining support vector machines with gold nanoparticle sensors and gas chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (GC-MS) can significantly discrimination between AC and SCC in the headspace of lung cancer subtypes cells 1 . Santonico et al. and his group explored the effect of two breath sampling method on classification accuracy of AC and SCC after combining GC-MS and gas sensor array for exhaled breath analysis. Their results claimed that the classification performance of endoscopic breath sampling (EBS) outperformed than bag breath sampling (BBS) and could achieve 75% accuracy. Unfortunately, given the complexity of the sampling, they only performed the gas analysis in small size sample 16 . In the same year, Mazzone et al. demonstrated the feasibility of classifying the exhaled breath of lung cancer patients with different histological subtypes through a colorimetric sensor array. They obtained excellent classification results using a backward step-down feature selection method before performing a logistic regression analysis. Nevertheless, it was regrettable that they were unable to qualitatively analyze the features due to the dye-analyte interaction principle of colorimetric sensors 17 . Recently, Handa et al. found the feasibility of decision trees algorithm for the identification of AC and SCC using ion mobility spectrometry. However, their classification results did not present details results about diagnostic ability, specificity, and sensitivity 18 . Most of the studies in breathomics analysis used algorithms alone to achieve the goal of distinguishing tumor histological subtypes, and they pay less attention to data pre-processing of the breathomics data to obtain exact information before conducting the regression or classification model. Studies have proven that data pre-processing is an indispensable part of multivariate analysis 19,20 . 

Data pre-processing is a series of operations before classification tasks, including outlier exclusion, missing data imputation, feature project, class balance. In this study, we will detail discuss the feature engineering and class balance, which are the most critical factors affecting the performance of the classification model. The breathomics data generated by the high-throughput analytical platforms contain redundant information such as mixture interference in the exhaled breath.

Title: Fast and automated biomarker detection in breath samples with machine learning
Snippet: Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in human breath can reveal a large spectrum of health conditions and can be used for fast, accurate and non-invasive diagnostics. Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) is used to measure VOCs, but its application is limited by expert-driven data analysis that is time-consuming, subjective and may introduce errors. We propose a machine learning-based system to perform GC-MS data analysis that exploits deep learning pattern recognition ability to learn and automatically detect VOCs directly from raw data, thus bypassing expert-led processing. We evaluate this new approach on clinical samples and with four types of convolutional neural networks (CNNs): VGG16, VGG-like, densely connected and residual CNNs. The proposed machine learning methods showed to outperform the expert-led analysis by detecting a significantly higher number of VOCs in just a fraction of time while maintaining high specificity. These results suggest that the proposed novel approach can help the large-scale deployment of breath-based diagnosis by reducing time and cost, and increasing accuracy and consistency.

Snippet: Recent advancements in machine learning have accelerated the application of breathomics for respiratory disease classification. These efforts leverage the high-dimensional and complex nature of exhaled VOCs and demonstrate the feasibility of non-invasive diagnostic modeling across a variety of pulmonary conditions. 

In a large-scale study targeting pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB), Fu et al. collected breath samples from 518 PTB patients and 887 controls using HPPI-TOF-MS. Using ensemble models such as XGBoost and random forest, the researchers achieved high performance in both validation and blinded test sets, with an AUC of 0.975, accuracy of 92.6%, and specificity of 93.0%, representing the robustness and scalability of breath-based machine learning models in infectious respiratory diseases 34 . 

For interstitial lung disease (ILD) classification, Massenet et al. analyzed breath VOC profiles from patients with systemic sclerosis (SSc) and systemic sclerosis-associated ILD (SSc-ILD) using thermal desorption comprehensive two-dimensional gas chromatography high-resolution mass spectrometry (TD-GC×GC-HRMS). From ~ 800 detected features, a partial least squares-discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) model identified nine discriminative VOCs and achieved an AUC of 0.82, sensitivity of 77%, and specificity of 100%. Importantly, the study demonstrated the feasibility of multicentric breathomics protocols and linked VOC profiles to pulmonary function metrics such as DLCO, reinforcing the physiological relevance of the predictive markers 35 . 

Most directly relevant to our study, Tian et al. developed classification models for COPD, asthma, and preserved ratio impaired spirometry (PRISm) using VOCs captured via portable micro gas chromatography. Involving 367 patients across multiple disease groups, the study identified specific VOC markers for differentiating COPD vs. asthma, PRISm vs. healthy, and other pairwise comparisons. Machine learning algorithms including random forest, support vector machine (SVM), and XGBoost were trained on both VOC features and clinical metadata. The optimal models yielded high classification accuracies across all disease pairs, illustrating the potential of breathomics in resolving clinically overlapping respiratory conditions 36 .

Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in breath can reflect the pathophysiological processes of disease, thereby having the potential to serve as a promising approach for diagnosing respiratory diseases. Can we identify VOC markers in breath with the potential to serve as classification indicators, and further establish learning models for the early detection of COPD, asthma, or PRISm patients? Title: Multistage Classification And Ensemble Learning Techniques For Automated Respiratory Sound Analysis: A Comprehensive Review
Snippet: A critical step in the classification of the respiratory signals is the preprocessing of such raw recordings of lung sounds contaminated with noise and artifacts, which are detrimental to the performance of classification. Aside from environmental noise and heart sounds interfering with recordings, variations in recording conditions are challenges that must be addressed before feature extraction and classification [26]. 

Denoising methods are usually applied for enhancement of quality in respiratory signals. Wavelet Transform (WT) is one of the most widespread methods used in the decomposition of lung sounds into different frequency bands on which noise are separated from useful signal components [27]. Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) is another method to be used, whereby it applies to extracting intrinsic mode functions that help segment respiratory sounds and background noise [28]. All these techniques tend to preserve important features of the signal. 

Feature extraction has been playing a very important role in differentiating between normal and abnormal lung sounds. Some of the time-domain features include zero-crossing rate, signal energy, and waveform variance, which would just provide the most elementary insights with respect to signal patterns [29]. However, frequency-based features are considered more informative because they focus on studying the spectral components. For the extraction of dominant frequency peaks in adventitious lung sounds, the method most often used is Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) [30]. Besides, time-frequency analysis methods such as Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) and Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs), give a more descriptive representation of non-stationary respiratory signals [31]. 

More than feature extraction, the transformation techniques complement the same stage in classification benefits. Such transformation techniques include Principal Component Analysis (PCA), which always features as a technique for reducing the dimensionality of features while still retaining the significant signal characteristics [32]. Independent Component Analysis (ICA) splits independent sound sources to clarify signals, improving the quality of lung sound representations [33]. All these preprocessing techniques adjust features to lift the performance level for machine learning models to ensure strong respiratory sound classification. 

The principles behind the classification of respiratory signals enhance or predispose the grounds for advanced engineering processing methods.
</snippet>

Title: Time-Localized Parametric Decomposition of Respiratory Airflow for Sub-Breath Analysis
Snippet: Both discrete and continuous wavelet transforms have been used to extract multiscale features for respiratory event detection [30], [31]. Wavelet coefficients provide a joint time-scale representation that captures irregularities and asymmetries across multiple resolutions, supporting robust classification when combined with oximetry or pressure data [32], [33]. However, the resulting coefficients represent distributions of signal energy rather than explicit waveform components, which makes it difficult to interpret them in terms of physiological events or parameters such as amplitude, onset, or duration [34], [35]. Wavelet-based approaches have been extensively applied for respiratory sound classification [36], [37], demonstrating their utility for energybased feature extraction, though the resulting representations remain challenging to interpret in terms of specific temporal events within individual breaths. 

Data-Driven and Dictionary-Based Approaches. Beyond analytic transforms, adaptive methods such as Matching Pursuit (MP) and K-SVD decompositions have been applied to other biosignals but only rarely to airflow [38]. These techniques reconstruct a signal by selecting or learning atoms from a dictionary, enabling flexible representation of transient patterns. In practice, however, the learned or chosen atoms describe statistical structure in the data and are not explicitly constrained by physiological or morphological models of breathing. Related approaches using empirical mode decomposition (EMD) have been applied to respiratory signals to isolate dominant oscillatory components [39], [40]. EMD and ensemble EMD (EEMD) have been used to extract respiratory rate from photoplethysmographic signals [41], [42] and to differentiate normal from adventitious respiratory sounds [43]. While these decompositions provide adaptive flexibility, the resulting intrinsic modes vary in frequency and phase across realizations, making cross-subject or cross-condition interpre-tation challenging. Moreover, as demonstrated in [37], hybrid approaches combining EMD with continuous wavelet transforms still produce scalogram-based energy representations rather than explicit temporal parameters. 

Morphological Analysis of Airflow Waveforms. Several studies have sought to characterize the overall morphology of the instantaneous airflow waveform using frequency-domain descriptors [16], [17], [18].

The respiratory phases were segmented by means of a zero-crossing detector applied to the flow signals, as described in our previous work [37]. After segmenting the respiratory phases from a subject's three pre-bronchodilator and three post-bronchodilator flow signals, the inspiratory and expiratory flow ranges were calculated as the differences between the maximum and minimum peak flows of all the inspiratory and expiratory phases, respectively. Flow ranges were divided into four quartiles, Q1-Q4, with Q1 including the lowest flows. In this way, a flow quartile was assigned to each respiratory phase, according to its peak flow (Fig 2). 

Acoustic component segmentation and characterization. After having segmented all the respiratory phases, the corresponding respiratory sound signals from the four recorded channels of a subject were analyzed, for acoustic component segmentation, using a new method that we have recently described in two previous studies, based on the analysis of the instantaneous frequency (IF) and envelope (IE) sequences [33], and the Hilbert spectrum time-frequency distribution [34]. The method is briefly described in this section. 

First, our automatic CAS detection algorithm [33] was applied to each respiratory sound signal. Based on the fact that the IF dispersion markedly decreases when CAS appear within a respiratory sound signal, that algorithm detected respiratory sound signal segments that were more likely to contain CAS. To do that, each respiratory sound signal was decomposed by ensemble empirical mode decomposition into a set of narrowband components for which the IF and IE sequences were calculated by means of the Hilbert transform. Then, a number of dispersion-based criteria were used on the IF sequences to detect respiratory sound signal segments with a lower IF dispersion. Each detected segment was characterized by means of a set of features extracted from the IF and IE sequences, including the mean and standard deviation IF. These features were used to classify respiratory sound signal segments as CAS segments or normal segments, using a support vector machine classifier. 

After detecting CAS and normal segments within a respiratory sound signal, the acoustic component segmentation was performed [34].

Title: Automated Quantitative Analysis of Capnogram Shape for COPD–Normal and COPD–CHF Classification
Snippet: We develop an approach to quantitative analysis of carbon dioxide concentration in exhaled breath, recorded as a function of time by capnography. The generated waveform-or capnogram-is currently used in clinical practice to establish the presence of respiration as well as determine respiratory rate and end-tidal CO2 concentration. The capnogram shape also has diagnostic value, but is presently assessed qualitatively, by visual inspection. Prior approaches to quantitatively characterizing the capnogram shape have explored the correlation of various geometric parameters with pulmonary function tests. These studies attempted to characterize the capnogram in normal subjects and patients with cardiopulmonary disease, but no consistent progress was made, and no translation into clinical practice was achieved. We apply automated quantitative analysis to discriminate between chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and congestive heart failure (CHF), and between COPD and normal. Capnograms were collected from 30 normal subjects, 56 COPD patients, and 53 CHF patients. We computationally extract four physiologically based capnogram features. Classification on a hold-out test set was performed by an ensemble of classifiers employing quadratic discriminant analysis, designed through cross validation on a labeled training set. Using 80 exhalations of each capnogram record in the test set, performance analysis with bootstrapping yields areas under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of 0.89 (95% CI: 0.72-0.96) for COPD/CHF classification, and 0.98 (95% CI: 0.82-1.0) for COPD/normal classification. This classification performance is obtained with a run time sufficiently fast for realtime monitoring.
</snippet>

Title: A machine learning algorithm for detecting abnormal patterns in continuous capnography and pulse oximetry monitoring
Snippet: Opioids are powerful painkillers which are often prescribed after surgery to treat severe pain. However, they come with several adverse effects such as Opioid-Induced Respiratory Depression (OIRD) [2][3][4]. OIRD can lead to severe and to catch true occurrences of respiratory depression without triggering false alarms. 

Continuous capnography and pulse oximetry tracings are affected by many patient-related factors, such as coughing, talking, moving, or equipment-related factors, such as sensor-or calibration errors. Furthermore, there is individual variability in both normal respiratory patterns and the patterns that may indicate respiratory depression. To create an effective alarm system, it is necessary to develop an algorithm that can interpret continuous data, filter out noise, recognize relevant patterns, and make reliable predictions of true events. With the rise of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI), the possibilities to accurately analyze capnography data have increased, yet we are still dealing with the challenge of imbalanced datasets, as explained below. True respiratory depression events are infrequent, as they represent irregularities in a generally regular breathing pattern. Normal breathing patterns are much more common than true respiratory depressions. This leads to an inherent class imbalance in the data. This imbalance can bias ML models towards the majority class, resulting in increased misclassifications. Therefore, solving these challenges is key to improving classification of continuous respiratory measurements. 

Time series classification (TSC) using a multi-stage approach offers a potential solution to the problem of imbalanced data sets. By initially focusing on the separation of normal breathing and abnormal patterns, we can remedy the class imbalance problem. Following initial classification, more complex models may be applied to the refined 'abnormal' dataset in a second stage of the analysis. This sequential method is known to enhance accuracy in anomaly detection and to improve computational efficiency [12,13]. This makes multi-stage TSC a practical and effective strategy for the classification of continuous capnography and pulse oximetry measurements. 

With this approach, the first stage model plays a vital role. The goal of this study is to determine the performance of such a first-stage TSC model.
</snippet>

Title: An Effective Machine Learning Approach for Classifying Artefact-Free and Distorted Capnogram Segments Using Simple Time-Domain Features
Snippet: Capnogram signal analysis has received considerable attention owing to its important applications in assessing cardiopulmonary functions. However, the automatic elimination of deformed parts of a capnogram waveform remains an open research problem. Herein, we introduce an automatic classification approach for discriminating artefact-free (regular) and distorted (irregular) segments of capnogram signals. The proposed features include Hjorth parameters and mean absolute deviation (MAD). The main advantage of these features is their simplicity, such that they can be employed in a computationally efficient machine learning algorithm. MATLAB simulation is conducted on 100 regular and 100 irregular segments of capnogram to extract the proposed and existing features, which are ranked based on the Pearson correlation coefficient, ${p}$ -value and area under receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. The naive Bayes, decision tree, random forest and support vector machine (SVM) classifiers are fed by the relatively highly ranked features, and the classification performance is assessed via ten-fold cross-validation. Besides the linear kernel SVM, the radial basis function (RBF) and polynomial kernel functions with different orders are also included in the current experiment. Results revealed the effectiveness of the Hjorth activity and MAD attributes when used with the fourth-order polynomial kernel-SVM classifier. The achieved accuracy, precision and specificity are 89%, 92.1%, and 91% outperforming the existing method by 2.5%, 5.6% and 7%, respectively. The simplicity of the proposed time-domain features is confirmed by the average total computational time of features extraction and classification phases which is only 13 ms instead of 19 ms in the case of incorporating both time- and frequency-domain features, indicating a reduction of 31.6%. It is envisaged that the proposed approach can be valuable if implemented with capnography devices for real-time and fully automated capnogram-based respiratory assessment. Even so, further research is recommended to enhance the classification performance through exploring more features and/or classifiers.
</snippet>

  • For capnograms: hand-crafted shape features with classical classifiers (QDA) or end-to-end CNNs; multi-stage time-series classifiers to handle rare abnormal events. <cite id="04d9653a-1">Physiology-informed features plus QDA ensembles achieve high AUROC in COPD/CHF vs COPD/normal classification</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-2">A multi-stage time-series classification approach separates normal vs abnormal patterns first to tackle class imbalance, then applies more complex models to the abnormal cohort</cite>.
  • For airflow/respiratory sounds: CNNs on spectrograms, MFCCs, or learned embeddings; hybrid models with oximetry/pressure; tree ensembles on engineered features; consider complex network/graph features for bronchial sounds. <cite id="8a8be054-4">Deep CNNs operating on spectrograms automatically recognize disease/abnormal lung sounds; automated segmentation extracts intensity/frequency parameters</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-1">Time–frequency features (STFT/MFCC) and dimensionality reduction (PCA/ICA) improve classification of respiratory sounds</cite>.
- Evaluation and robustness:
  • Report per-breath and per-subject metrics; cross-visit and cross-center validation; stratify by sampling modality and device generation (bag vs endobronchial sampling can change accuracy/bias). <cite id="5a5d82c9-1">Endoscopic breath sampling outperformed bag breath sampling in histology subtype classification and achieved 75% accuracy, underscoring sampling-method effects</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-3">Multi-center TD-GC×GC-HRMS protocols achieved high performance (AUC 0.82, 77% sens, 100% spec) and linked VOC markers to DLCO</cite>.
  • Address class imbalance and noise explicitly for anomaly detection (e.g., respiratory depression). <cite id="04d9653a-2">Opioid-induced respiratory depression is rare; multi-stage time-series classification mitigates imbalance by first separating normal vs abnormal patterns, improving anomaly detection efficiency</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-1">Variations in recording conditions and overlapping heart sounds require denoising and segmentation to avoid performance degradation</cite>.
  • For breathomics, include metabolite ratio features and background drift normalization; use imputation and outlier removal; validate model generalization across GC–MS platforms. <cite id="5a5d82c9-1">Pre-processing (outlier exclusion, missing data imputation, feature projection, and class balance) is indispensable; decision-tree pipelines improved with feature selection and balancing</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-2">Deep learning on raw GC–MS chromatograms bypasses subjective expert steps and increases consistency and throughput</cite>.

3) Pattern-finding by modality: concrete techniques and examples
- Breathomics (VOCs): 
  • Patterns: differential abundance of lipid peroxidation products, aldehydes, alkanes; VOC clusters aligning with disease pathways. <cite id="5a5d82c9-0">Interpretable ML on GC–MS breath VOCs identified key VOCs driving asthma/bronchiectasis/COPD predictions, enabling candidate biomarker discovery</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-3">In PTB, ensemble models on ~800 HRMS features achieved AUC 0.975 with high specificity; ILD classification identified nine VOCs with AUC 0.82 and 100% specificity</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-4">In a 367-patient cross-sectional study, nine VOCs separated COPD from healthy, and five VOCs asthma vs healthy; RF best discriminated COPD vs healthy (AUC 0.92)</cite>.
  • Practical steps: align chromatograms, extract m/z peaks and areas; normalize to breath depth/time and background blanks; select features via mutual information/recursive feature elimination or permutation importance; use ensembles with SHAP. <cite id="5a5d82c9-2">Deep CNNs learned to detect VOCs directly from raw chromatograms, detecting more VOCs faster with high specificity than expert-driven workflows</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-0">SHAP-based interpretability tied specific VOCs to predictions, supporting clinical translation</cite>.
- Respiratory airflow and sounds:
  • Patterns: amplitude variability, energy shifts, spectral peak emergence, crackle/rale bursts, asymmetric expiratory flow limitation, and periodic breathing. <cite id="8a8be054-0">Mean amplitude, variance, RMS, peak-to-peak, and zero-crossing rate distinguish normal from hypoventilation and characterize periodic breathing</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-1">FFT yields dominant frequency peaks; STFT/MFCCs capture nonstationary bursts, and PCA/ICA condense structure for ML</cite> <cite id="8a8be54-3">Hilbert-based instantaneous frequency/envelope analysis identifies crackles/rales segments, enabling time-localized classification</cite>.
  • Practical steps: denoise with wavelets/EMD; segment breaths via zero crossings and flow thresholds; compute spectral features and entropy; build RF/XGBoost or CNNs on spectrograms; for bronchodilator response, analyze flow quartiles per phase. <cite id="8a8be054-1">Wavelet/EMD denoising and feature extraction improve classification of normal vs adventitious sounds</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-3">Zero-crossing segmentation plus Hilbert-spectrum–based detection/classification of crackles/rales supports within-breath analysis tied to bronchodilator response</cite>.
- Capnography (PETCO2 waveform):
  • Patterns: phase III alveolar plateau slope (Slopes A–D), diffusion/dispersion artifacts, rebreathing loops, PETCO2 trends reflecting hypoventilation or shunting, and distinct shapes in COPD vs CHF vs normal. <cite id="04d9653a-0">Capnogram morphological features like slope/angle and peak values correlate with FEV1/FVC and help differentiate obstructive and restrictive lung diseases</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-1">Four physiologically based features plus QDA ensembles achieved AUROC 0.89 (COPD/CHF) and 0.98 (COPD/normal)</cite>.
  • Practical steps: detect phase boundaries; compute PETCO2 end-tidal and phase III slope; apply Hjorth activity and MAD to classify artefact-free vs distorted segments; use time–domain features with fast SVMs for real-time filtering. <cite id="04d9653a-3">Hjorth activity and mean absolute deviation features with polynomial-kernel SVMs achieved 89% accuracy/92.1% precision/91% specificity in artefact classification, with 13 ms per segment processing</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-4">Automated artefact-free vs distorted segment classification is essential before disease modeling and can be implemented for real-time capnogram assessment</cite>.
  • Anomaly detection: multi-stage TSC to detect opioid-induced respiratory depression by learning normal baseline dynamics, gating on movement/sensor health, and using synthetic minority oversampling or weighted losses; monitor false-positive rates. <cite id="04d9653a-2">Multi-stage time-series classification addresses class imbalance and recognizes relevant patterns in continuous capnography/SpO2, enabling faster anomaly detection</cite>.

4) Advanced modeling and anomaly/outlier detection
- Deep learning for temporal patterns: CNNs on spectrograms of airflow/sounds learn morphological invariants; RNN/LSTM/Transformer variants capture long-range breath-to-breath dependencies and transitions; end-to-end models on volumetric capnography can replace hand-crafted features. <cite id="8a8be054-4">Spectrogram CNNs end-to-end detect respiratory disease and abnormal sounds, supported by automated segmentation of time labels</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-0">Transformed volumetric capnography integrated with AI improves standardization and accuracy for diagnosis</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-1">End-to-end models inputting raw capnograms differentiated COPD-normal and COPD-CHF</cite>.
- Anomaly/outlier detection: density-based clustering (e.g., DBSCAN) on feature embeddings; autoencoders to reconstruct normal breath patterns and flag high-reconstruction-error segments; multi-stage pipelines separate normal vs abnormal first to reduce imbalance impact. <cite id="04d9653a-2">Multi-stage TSC with an initial separator of normal vs abnormal improves class imbalance handling and accuracy in anomaly detection for continuous capnography and SpO2</cite>.
- Interpretable pattern discovery: SHAP/feature attribution for breathomics; Hilbert IF/IE dispersion for identifying crackle/rale bursts in sounds; global shape descriptors in capnograms (phase III slope) map to physiology (airway calibre, alveolar diffusion). <cite id="5a5d82c9-0">SHAP identifies VOCs driving predictions in breathomics, enabling candidate marker discovery</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-3">Lower IF dispersion marks crackle/rale segments, providing interpretable criteria for abnormal component detection</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-0">Phase III slope/angle and peak features translate to spirometric indices (FEV1/FVC) and disease categories</cite>.

5) Validation, drift, and deployment considerations
- Internal vs external validation: stratify by site/device/disease stage; use blinded sets for capnography/breathomics to confirm generalization; ensure sampling modality consistency in breathomics. <cite id="5a5d82c9-3">Evaluations across validation and blinded test sets achieved AUC 0.975 and 92.6% accuracy for TB, demonstrating robustness and scalability of breath-based ML models</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-1">Sampling modality affects performance (EBS > BBS in one study), and careful feature selection and class balancing are critical</cite>.
- Drift and artifacts: implement runtime artifact rejection (motion/leak detection) and reference-channel gating; for breathomics, baseline correction and blank-subtraction; capnogram pipelines classify artefact-free vs distorted segments before analytics. <cite id="8a8be054-1">EMD/wavelet denoising and segmentation improve robustness to noise and interference in respiratory signals</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-3">Real-time artefact classification with simple time-domain features enables automated capnogram assessment</cite>.
- Clinical translation: link pattern features to physiology (e.g., VOC markers to DLCO; capnogram slope to FEV1) and provide decision support with explainability; track sensitivity/specificity and clinically meaningful effect sizes, not only accuracy. <cite id="5a5d82c9-3">ILD studies linked discriminative VOCs to DLCO and demonstrated multicentric protocols, reinforcing physiological relevance</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-1">Physiology-grounded capnogram features yield clinically actionable discrimination with high AUROC and fast runtimes</cite>.

6) A practical step-by-step recipe (choose your modality)
- Step 1: Record and log metadata
  • For VOCs: capture GC–MS or micro-GC runs with breath type (bag vs EBS), duration, tidal volume/flow, room background blanks, and clinical labels. <cite id="5a5d82c9-1">Sampling method and preprocessing critically affect performance; endobronchial sampling outperformed bag sampling in subtype classification</cite>.
  • For airflow/sounds: record flow/pressure and/or stereo/omni acoustic sensors synchronized with oximetry; note ambient noise, patient position, and medication. <cite id="8a8be054-1">Environmental noise and heart sounds require denoising before classification</cite>.
  • For capnography: collect continuous PETCO2 with SpO2; log ventilator settings, coughs/locomotion events, and device calibration times. <cite id="04d9653a-2">Continuous monitoring is affected by movement/calibration; ML must interpret long streams and handle imbalance</cite>.
- Step 2: Preprocess to extract patterns
  • Breathomics: align chromatograms; remove outliers and blanks; normalize per breath; correct baseline drift. <cite id="5a5d82c9-2">Deep learning directly on raw chromatograms bypasses subjective expert processing, increasing speed and specificity</cite>.
  • Airflow/sounds: denoise with wavelet/EMD; segment breaths via zero-crossing/flow thresholds; compute time/frequency features and entropy; for sounds, compute IF/IE and dispersion to localize abnormal components. <cite id="8a8be054-1">Wavelet/EMD preserve morphology while separating noise; FFT/STFT/MFCCs yield spectral features</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-3">Hilbert-spectrum–based detection of crackles/rales segments supports event localization</cite>.
  • Capnography: detect phases; compute PETCO2 end-tidal and phase III slope; classify artefact-free vs distorted segments using simple features for real-time filtering. <cite id="04d9653a-1">Physiologically based features enable fast, accurate discrimination between COPD/CHF and COPD/normal</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-3">Hjorth activity and MAD with SVM provide fast artefact classification (13 ms per segment)</cite>.
- Step 3: Feature selection and model choice
  • Breathomics: select VOC peaks and ratios; use tree ensembles with SHAP; consider deep CNNs on chromatogram tiles. <cite id="5a5d82c9-0">Ensemble models and SHAP identify key VOCs for asthma/COPD/bronchiectasis</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-2">CNNs on raw GC–MS detect more VOCs reliably than expert analysis</cite>.
  • Airflow/sounds: combine time/frequency features and morphology-derived statistics; train RF/XGBoost or CNNs on spectrograms; for bronchodilator response, stratify by flow quartiles. <cite id="8a8be054-1">Time–frequency features and dimensionality reduction improve classification of adventitious vs normal sounds</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-3">Flow quartile segmentation enables within-breath assessment of bronchodilator response</cite>.
  • Capnography: engineer phase/slope/shape features; train QDA ensembles or CNNs; deploy artefact classifiers first to reduce imbalance. <cite id="04d9653a-1">Four capnogram features with QDA ensembles yield AUROC 0.89–0.98</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-2">Multi-stage TSC improves anomaly detection under class imbalance</cite>.
- Step 4: Evaluate and iterate
  • Use cross-subject, cross-site, and blinded cohorts; report sensitivity/specificity and clinically interpretable effect sizes; retrain on new sensor generations/sampling modalities. <cite id="5a5d82c9-3">Blinded tests with ensemble models achieved AUC 0.975 and 92.6% accuracy for TB, with multicenter feasibility</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-1">Sampling modality influences performance, requiring external validation and feature engineering</cite>.
- Step 5: Deploy and monitor
  • Add runtime artifact rejection, drift detection, and explainability (SHAP for breathomics, IF/IE thresholds for sounds, shape/slope flags for capnography); set actionable thresholds and audit false alarms. <cite id="04d9653a-3">Real-time artefact classification enables automated capnogram-based assessment</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-0">SHAP-based interpretability reinforces model outputs and suggests biochemical markers</cite>.

7) Disease-focused pointers to recognizable patterns
- Asthma vs COPD and PRISm: breathomics models consistently separate these groups using VOC markers; airflow/respiratory sound analyses show increased high-frequency energy and crackle prevalence in small-airway disease. <cite id="5a5d82c9-3">VOC-based models (RF/XGBoost) on micro-GC data identified specific VOCs for COPD vs asthma and PRISm vs healthy, with high accuracies across disease pairs</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-1">Spectral energy and morphology features differentiate adventitious from normal lung sounds, supporting small-airway disease detection</cite>.
- Interstitial lung disease (ILD) and pulmonary hypertension: breathomics markers correlate with DLCO; capnogram patterns reflect diffusion impairment and right-heart involvement. <cite id="5a5d82c9-3">TD-GC×GC-HRMS models identified nine VOCs with AUC 0.82, 77% sensitivity, and 100% specificity, linked to DLCO</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-0">Capnogram features such as phase III slope/angle correlate with FEV1/FVC and differentiate obstructive vs restrictive disease</cite>.
- Opioid-induced respiratory depression: continuous monitoring pipelines detect deviations from normal cycle morphology and PETCO2 dynamics; multi-stage anomaly detectors reduce false alarms. <cite id="04d9653a-2">Imbalanced data and irregularities require multi-stage time-series classification; runtime is suitable for real-time monitoring</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-0">Zero-crossing and energy-based features capture hypoventilation and periodic irregularities</cite>.
- Tuberculosis and other infections: ensemble models trained on high-throughput mass spec profiles deliver high AUROC and accuracy; multicenter validation supports scalability. <cite id="5a5d82c9-3">For PTB (N=518 PTB, 887 controls), ensemble models achieved AUC 0.975 and 92.6% accuracy with high specificity</cite>.

Summary: To find patterns in breath data, align preprocessing to your modality’s noise and physiological overlap, segment breath cycles and events, engineer features that capture the hypothesized pattern (VOC composition, airflow/sound morphology, capnogram shape/dynamics), and model with tree ensembles (with SHAP/attribute masks) or deep CNNs on spectrograms/chromatograms; validate across sites/devices and clinical cohorts, and add runtime artifact/reconstruction-error monitoring for anomalies. <cite id="5a5d82c9-0">Interpretable ML on breath VOCs reveals disease-linked chemical patterns and supports clinical plausibility</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-1">Respiratory sound/airflow pipelines use denoising and time–frequency features to expose pathological patterns</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-1">Capnogram shape features and ensembles detect clinically relevant differences with high AUROC</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-2">Deep learning on raw breath-chemistry traces automates biomarker detection faster and more consistently than expert pipelines</cite> <cite id="04d9653a-2">Anomaly detection for respiratory depression benefits from multi-stage time-series classification to handle rare events and noise</cite>.

Limitations and next steps: Breathomics performance varies with sampling modality and platform; airflow/sound analyses can be confounded by recording conditions and heart sounds; capnogram interpretation requires robust artefact rejection. Address these by including modality/ device as covariates, deploying automated artefact filters, and conducting multi-center blinded validation. Emerging directions include learning breath-specific transformers and self-supervised embeddings across modalities, and integrating multimodal streams (flow + sound + PETCO2 + VOCs) for ensemble pattern discovery. <cite id="5a5d82c9-1">Sampling method (EBS vs BBS) affects classification accuracy and should be standardized or included in models</cite> <cite id="8a8be054-1">Variations in recording conditions and overlapping sounds necessitate denoising and segmentation for robust classification</cite> <cite id="5a5d82c9-3">Physiology-linked VOC markers and multi-center protocols show feasibility, but external validation remains essential</cite>.

Title: A baseline study of interpretable machine learning using GC-MS breath VOCs for classifying asthma, bronchiectasis, and COPD
Snippet: We present a reproducible, interpretable machine learning baseline for classifying asthma, bronchiectasis, and COPD from a public GC-MS dataset of exhaled breath VOCs. Across seven supervised classifiers, particularly ensemble-based models such as XGBoost, we observed strong diagnostic performance across multiple evaluation metrics. The incorporation of SHAP-based interpretability further enabled the identification of key VOCs driving disease-specific predictions, providing candidate biochemical markers and reinforcing the biological plausibility of model outputs. These results underscore the utility of breathomics not only as a practical diagnostic alternative to invasive or subjective diagnostic tools but also as a pathway toward transparent and explainable respiratory disease classification. By establishing this reproducible and interpretable baseline, our work provides a reference point for future methodological advancements and external validation in breathomics-based diagnostics.

Title: Exploratory study on classification of lung cancer subtypes through a combined K-nearest neighbor classifier in breathomics
Snippet: problem of lung cancer subtypes in vitro 15 . In 2012, Barash et al. proved that combining support vector machines with gold nanoparticle sensors and gas chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (GC-MS) can significantly discrimination between AC and SCC in the headspace of lung cancer subtypes cells 1 . Santonico et al. and his group explored the effect of two breath sampling method on classification accuracy of AC and SCC after combining GC-MS and gas sensor array for exhaled breath analysis. Their results claimed that the classification performance of endoscopic breath sampling (EBS) outperformed than bag breath sampling (BBS) and could achieve 75% accuracy. Unfortunately, given the complexity of the sampling, they only performed the gas analysis in small size sample 16 . In the same year, Mazzone et al. demonstrated the feasibility of classifying the exhaled breath of lung cancer patients with different histological subtypes through a colorimetric sensor array. They obtained excellent classification results using a backward step-down feature selection method before performing a logistic regression analysis. Nevertheless, it was regrettable that they were unable to qualitatively analyze the features due to the dye-analyte interaction principle of colorimetric sensors 17 . Recently, Handa et al. found the feasibility of decision trees algorithm for the identification of AC and SCC using ion mobility spectrometry. However, their classification results did not present details results about diagnostic ability, specificity, and sensitivity 18 . Most of the studies in breathomics analysis used algorithms alone to achieve the goal of distinguishing tumor histological subtypes, and they pay less attention to data pre-processing of the breathomics data to obtain exact information before conducting the regression or classification model. Studies have proven that data pre-processing is an indispensable part of multivariate analysis 19,20 . 

Data pre-processing is a series of operations before classification tasks, including outlier exclusion, missing data imputation, feature project, class balance. In this study, we will detail discuss the feature engineering and class balance, which are the most critical factors affecting the performance of the classification model. The breathomics data generated by the high-throughput analytical platforms contain redundant information such as mixture interference in the exhaled breath.

Title: Fast and automated biomarker detection in breath samples with machine learning
Snippet: Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in human breath can reveal a large spectrum of health conditions and can be used for fast, accurate and non-invasive diagnostics. Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) is used to measure VOCs, but its application is limited by expert-driven data analysis that is time-consuming, subjective and may introduce errors. We propose a machine learning-based system to perform GC-MS data analysis that exploits deep learning pattern recognition ability to learn and automatically detect VOCs directly from raw data, thus bypassing expert-led processing. We evaluate this new approach on clinical samples and with four types of convolutional neural networks (CNNs): VGG16, VGG-like, densely connected and residual CNNs. The proposed machine learning methods showed to outperform the expert-led analysis by detecting a significantly higher number of VOCs in just a fraction of time while maintaining high specificity. These results suggest that the proposed novel approach can help the large-scale deployment of breath-based diagnosis by reducing time and cost, and increasing accuracy and consistency.

Title: A baseline study of interpretable machine learning using GC-MS breath VOCs for classifying asthma, bronchiectasis, and COPD
Snippet: Recent advancements in machine learning have accelerated the application of breathomics for respiratory disease classification. These efforts leverage the high-dimensional and complex nature of exhaled VOCs and demonstrate the feasibility of non-invasive diagnostic modeling across a variety of pulmonary conditions. 

In a large-scale study targeting pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB), Fu et al. collected breath samples from 518 PTB patients and 887 controls using HPPI-TOF-MS. Using ensemble models such as XGBoost and random forest, the researchers achieved high performance in both validation and blinded test sets, with an AUC of 0.975, accuracy of 92.6%, and specificity of 93.0%, representing the robustness and scalability of breath-based machine learning models in infectious respiratory diseases 34 . 

For interstitial lung disease (ILD) classification, Massenet et al. analyzed breath VOC profiles from patients with systemic sclerosis (SSc) and systemic sclerosis-associated ILD (SSc-ILD) using thermal desorption comprehensive two-dimensional gas chromatography high-resolution mass spectrometry (TD-GC×GC-HRMS). From ~ 800 detected features, a partial least squares-discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) model identified nine discriminative VOCs and achieved an AUC of 0.82, sensitivity of 77%, and specificity of 100%. Importantly, the study demonstrated the feasibility of multicentric breathomics protocols and linked VOC profiles to pulmonary function metrics such as DLCO, reinforcing the physiological relevance of the predictive markers 35 . 

Most directly relevant to our study, Tian et al. developed classification models for COPD, asthma, and preserved ratio impaired spirometry (PRISm) using VOCs captured via portable micro gas chromatography. Involving 367 patients across multiple disease groups, the study identified specific VOC markers for differentiating COPD vs. asthma, PRISm vs. healthy, and other pairwise comparisons. Machine learning algorithms including random forest, support vector machine (SVM), and XGBoost were trained on both VOC features and clinical metadata. The optimal models yielded high classification accuracies across all disease pairs, illustrating the potential of breathomics in resolving clinically overlapping respiratory conditions 36 .

Title: Exhaled volatile organic compounds as novel biomarkers for early detection of COPD, asthma, and PRISm: a cross-sectional study
Snippet: Globally, chronic respiratory diseases have become the third leading cause of death, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma, and have been threatening human life for a long time. To alleviate the disease burden, it is crucial to develop rapid and convenient screening methods for COPD, preserved ratio impaired spirometry (PRISm), and asthma. Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in breath can reflect the pathophysiological processes of disease, thereby having the potential to serve as a promising approach for diagnosing respiratory diseases. Can we identify VOC markers in breath with the potential to serve as classification indicators, and further establish learning models for the early detection of COPD, asthma, or PRISm patients? This is a cross-sectional study in which exhaled breath samples were collected from 184 patients with COPD, 66 patients with asthma, 72 PRISm individuals, and 45 healthy individuals. From August 2023 to June 2024, the breath samples were analyzed using portable micro gas chromatography (CXBA-Alpha, ChromX Health Co., Ltd.). Potential VOC markers for classification were identified by univariate and multivariate analyses. Subsequently, classification models were established by machine learning algorithms, based on these VOC markers along with baseline characteristics. The sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of these models were calculated to assess their overall discriminatory performance. A total of 367 patients were enrolled in our study. We identified nine VOCs distinguishing COPD patients from healthy controls, nine VOCs differentiating the PRISm population from healthy controls, five VOCs separating asthma patients from healthy controls, five VOCs distinguishing COPD patients from asthma patients, and seven VOCs differentiating the PRISm population from asthma patients based on breathomics feature selection. We utilized five algorithms to establish diagnostic models and selected the optimal one among them. The random forest model best distinguished COPD from healthy controls with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.92 ± 0.01. documents.title: A baseline study of interpretable machine learning using GC-MS breath VOCs for classifying asthma, bronchiectasis, and COPD
documents.snippet: We present a reproducible, interpretable machine learning baseline for classifying asthma, bronchiectasis, and COPD from a public GC-MS dataset of exhaled breath VOCs. Across seven supervised classifiers, particularly ensemble-based models such as XGBoost, we observed strong diagnostic performance across multiple evaluation metrics. The incorporation of SHAP-based interpretability further enabled the identification of key VOCs driving disease-specific predictions, providing candidate biochemical markers and reinforcing the biological plausibility of model outputs. These results underscore the utility of breathomics not only as a practical diagnostic alternative to invasive or subjective diagnostic tools but also as a pathway toward transparent and explainable respiratory disease classification. By establishing this reproducible and interpretable baseline, our work provides a reference point for future methodological advancements and external validation in breathomics-based diagnostics.
