In 2012, Barash et al. proved that combining support vector machines with gold nanoparticle sensors and gas chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (GC-MS) can significantly discrimination between AC and SCC in the headspace of lung cancer subtypes cells 1 . Santonico et al. and his group explored the effect of two breath sampling method on classification accuracy of AC and SCC after combining GC-MS and gas sensor array for exhaled breath analysis. Their results claimed that the classification performance of endoscopic breath sampling (EBS) outperformed than bag breath sampling (BBS) and could achieve 75% accuracy. Unfortunately, given the complexity of the sampling, they only performed the gas analysis in small size sample 16 . In the same year, Mazzone et al. demonstrated the feasibility of classifying the exhaled breath of lung cancer patients with different histological subtypes through a colorimetric sensor array. They obtained excellent classification results using a backward step-down feature selection method before performing a logistic regression analysis. Nevertheless, it was regrettable that they were unable to qualitatively analyze the features due to the dye-analyte interaction principle of colorimetric sensors 17 . Recently, Handa et al. found the feasibility of decision trees algorithm for the identification of AC and SCC using ion mobility spectrometry. However, their classification results did not present details results about diagnostic ability, specificity, and sensitivity 18 . Most of the studies in breathomics analysis used algorithms alone to achieve the goal of distinguishing tumor histological subtypes, and they pay less attention to data pre-processing of the breathomics data to obtain exact information before conducting the regression or classification model. Studies have proven that data pre-processing is an indispensable part of multivariate analysis 19,20 . 

Data pre-processing is a series of operations before classification tasks, including outlier exclusion, missing data imputation, feature project, class balance. In this study, we will detail discuss the feature engineering and class balance, which are the most critical factors affecting the performance of the classification model. The breathomics data generated by the high-throughput analytical platforms contain redundant information such as mixture interference in the exhaled breath.

documents.title: Fast and automated biomarker detection in breath samples with machine learning
documents.snippet: Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in human breath can reveal a large spectrum of health conditions and can be used for fast, accurate and non-invasive diagnostics. Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) is used to measure VOCs, but its application is limited by expert-driven data analysis that is time-consuming, subjective and may introduce errors. We propose a machine learning-based system to perform GC-MS data analysis that exploits deep learning pattern recognition ability to learn and automatically detect VOCs directly from raw data, thus bypassing expert-led processing. We evaluate this new approach on clinical samples and with four types of convolutional neural networks (CNNs): VGG16, VGG-like, densely connected and residual CNNs. The proposed machine learning methods showed to outperform the expert-led analysis by detecting a significantly higher number of VOCs in just a fraction of time while maintaining high specificity. These results suggest that the proposed novel approach can help the large-scale deployment of breath-based diagnosis by reducing time and cost, and increasing accuracy and consistency.

Title: Multistage Classification And Ensemble Learning Techniques For Automated Respiratory Sound Analysis: A Comprehensive Review
Snippet: A critical step in the classification of the respiratory signals is the preprocessing of such raw recordings of lung sounds contaminated with noise and artifacts, which are detrimental to the performance of classification. Aside from environmental noise and heart sounds interfering with recordings, variations in recording conditions are challenges that must be addressed before feature extraction and classification [26]. 

Denoising methods are usually applied for enhancement of quality in respiratory signals. Wavelet Transform (WT) is one of the most widespread methods used in the decomposition of lung sounds into different frequency bands on which noise are separated from useful signal components [27]. Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) is another method to be used, whereby it applies to extracting intrinsic mode functions that help segment respiratory sounds and background noise [28]. All these techniques tend to preserve important features of the signal. 

Feature extraction has been playing a very important role in differentiating between normal and abnormal lung sounds. Some of the time-domain features include zero-crossing rate, signal energy, and waveform variance, which would just provide the most elementary insights with respect to signal patterns [29]. However, frequency-based features are considered more informative because they focus on studying the spectral components. For the extraction of dominant frequency peaks in adventitious lung sounds, the method most often used is Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) [30]. Besides, time-frequency analysis methods such as Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) and Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs), give a more descriptive representation of non-stationary respiratory signals [31]. 

More than feature extraction, the transformation techniques complement the same stage in classification benefits. Such transformation techniques include Principal Component Analysis (PCA), which always features as a technique for reducing the dimensionality of features while still retaining the significant signal characteristics [32]. Independent Component Analysis (ICA) splits independent sound sources to clarify signals, improving the quality of lung sound representations [33]. All these preprocessing techniques adjust features to lift the performance level for machine learning models to ensure strong respiratory sound classification. 

The principles behind the classification of respiratory signals enhance or predispose the grounds for advanced engineering processing methods.

Title: Time-Localized Parametric Decomposition of Respiratory Airflow for Sub-Breath Analysis
Snippet: Both discrete and continuous wavelet transforms have been used to extract multiscale features for respiratory event detection [30], [31]. Wavelet coefficients provide a joint time-scale representation that captures irregularities and asymmetries across multiple resolutions, supporting robust classification when combined with oximetry or pressure data [32], [33]. However, the resulting coefficients represent distributions of signal energy rather than explicit waveform components, which makes it difficult to interpret them in terms of physiological events or parameters such as amplitude, onset, or duration [34], [35]. Wavelet-based approaches have been extensively applied for respiratory sound classification [36], [37], demonstrating their utility for energybased feature extraction, though the resulting representations remain challenging to interpret in terms of specific temporal events within individual breaths. 

Data-Driven and Dictionary-Based Approaches. Beyond analytic transforms, adaptive methods such as Matching Pursuit (MP) and K-SVD decompositions have been applied to other biosignals but only rarely to airflow [38]. These techniques reconstruct a signal by selecting or learning atoms from a dictionary, enabling flexible representation of transient patterns. In practice, however, the learned or chosen atoms describe statistical structure in the data and are not explicitly constrained by physiological or morphological models of breathing. Related approaches using empirical mode decomposition (EMD) have been applied to respiratory signals to isolate dominant oscillatory components [39], [40]. EMD and ensemble EMD (EEMD) have been used to extract respiratory rate from photoplethysmographic signals [41], [42] and to differentiate normal from adventitious respiratory sounds [43]. While these decompositions provide adaptive flexibility, the resulting intrinsic modes vary in frequency and phase across realizations, making cross-subject or cross-condition interpre-tation challenging. Moreover, as demonstrated in [37], hybrid approaches combining EMD with continuous wavelet transforms still produce scalogram-based energy representations rather than explicit temporal parameters. 

Morphological Analysis of Airflow Waveforms. Several studies have sought to characterize the overall morphology of the instantaneous airflow waveform using frequency-domain descriptors [16], [17], [18].

Title: Novel approach to continuous adventitious respiratory sound analysis for the assessment of bronchodilator response
Snippet: Segmentation of respiratory phases and definition of flow quartiles. The respiratory phases were segmented by means of a zero-crossing detector applied to the flow signals, as described in our previous work [37]. After segmenting the respiratory phases from a subject's three pre-bronchodilator and three post-bronchodilator flow signals, the inspiratory and expiratory flow ranges were calculated as the differences between the maximum and minimum peak flows of all the inspiratory and expiratory phases, respectively. Flow ranges were divided into four quartiles, Q1-Q4, with Q1 including the lowest flows. In this way, a flow quartile was assigned to each respiratory phase, according to its peak flow (Fig 2). 

Acoustic component segmentation and characterization. After having segmented all the respiratory phases, the corresponding respiratory sound signals from the four recorded channels of a subject were analyzed, for acoustic component segmentation, using a new method that we have recently described in two previous studies, based on the analysis of the instantaneous frequency (IF) and envelope (IE) sequences [33], and the Hilbert spectrum time-frequency distribution [34]. The method is briefly described in this section. 

First, our automatic CAS detection algorithm [33] was applied to each respiratory sound signal. Based on the fact that the IF dispersion markedly decreases when CAS appear within a respiratory sound signal, that algorithm detected respiratory sound signal segments that were more likely to contain CAS. To do that, each respiratory sound signal was decomposed by ensemble empirical mode decomposition into a set of narrowband components for which the IF and IE sequences were calculated by means of the Hilbert transform. Then, a number of dispersion-based criteria were used on the IF sequences to detect respiratory sound signal segments with a lower IF dispersion. Each detected segment was characterized by means of a set of features extracted from the IF and IE sequences, including the mean and standard deviation IF. These features were used to classify respiratory sound signal segments as CAS segments or normal segments, using a support vector machine classifier. 

After detecting CAS and normal segments within a respiratory sound signal, the acoustic component segmentation was performed [34].

Title: Construction and Validation of an Automatic Segmentation Method for Respiratory Sound Time Labels
Snippet: The rapid development of artificial intelligence enables the identification of previously undetectable patterns in medical imaging and signal data, thereby improving the diagnosis of lung diseases [4][5][6]. Several algorithms have been validated for the robust automation capabilities in the segmentation of respiratory sounds. For example, Huang et al. proposed a technique for the detection and classification of respiratory sounds using vesicular sounds and crackle peak detection [7]. Through quantitative analysis of respiratory sounds, clinicians can differentiate between different types of moist rales, determine their timing within the breathing cycle, and assess their severity. The study conducted by Huang et al. employed an artificial intelligence in terms of deep learning methodology to transform lung sounds into two-dimensional spectrograms and used convolutional neural networks (CNN) for end-to-end recognition of respiratory system diseases or abnormal lung sounds [8]. To achieve segmentation results that align with the sequential nature of respiratory sounds, the author proposes a Python Package called TSSEARCH, which integrates subsequence search and time series similarity measurement with sequence timing models [9]. 

The collected respiratory sounds can be objectively analyzed through computerized intelligent analysis, allowing the signals to be decomposed into different intensities and frequencies for a more accurate characterization of such signals. This technology enables a more objective analysis of respiratory sounds and noise to better understand them [10]. Techniques used in other applications include the determination of breath sound boundaries, feature extraction of breath sounds and noise, differentiation between expiratory and inspiratory phases, and reduction of noise interference. To characterize breath sound parameters in a more accurate way, artificial intelligence algorithms will provide a more intelligent approach used in the overall deciphering process. 

Complex network analysis can be applied to the study of bioacoustics signals and bronchial breath sounds. By utilizing machine learning techniques that extract graph features, the intensity and frequency of respiratory sounds can be measured, which represent fundamental characteristics of sound during the breathing process [11]. In addition, the electronic stethoscope was used to digitize respiratory sounds with full patient cooperation in a quiet environment, while providing hardware and software tools to analyze the raw data. 

The present study introduced a novel approach for the automated segmentation of respiratory sounds and extraction of fundamental frequency and intensity parameters.

A critical step in the classification of the respiratory signals is the preprocessing of such raw recordings of lung sounds contaminated with noise and artifacts, which are detrimental to the performance of classification. Aside from environmental noise and heart sounds interfering with recordings, variations in recording conditions are challenges that must be addressed before feature extraction and classification [26]. 

Denoising methods are usually applied for enhancement of quality in respiratory signals. Wavelet Transform (WT) is one of the most widespread methods used in the decomposition of lung sounds into different frequency bands on which noise are separated from useful signal components [27]. Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) is another method to be used, whereby it applies to extracting intrinsic mode functions that help segment respiratory sounds and background noise [28]. All these techniques tend to preserve important features of the signal. 

Feature extraction has been playing a very important role in differentiating between normal and abnormal lung sounds. Some of the time-domain features include zero-crossing rate, signal energy, and waveform variance, which would just provide the most elementary insights with respect to signal patterns [29]. However, frequency-based features are considered more informative because they focus on studying the spectral components. For the extraction of dominant frequency peaks in adventitious lung sounds, the method most often used is Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) [30]. Besides, time-frequency analysis methods such as Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) and Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs), give a more descriptive representation of non-stationary respiratory signals [31]. 

More than feature extraction, the transformation techniques complement the same stage in classification benefits. Such transformation techniques include Principal Component Analysis (PCA), which always features as a technique for reducing the dimensionality of features while still retaining the significant signal characteristics [32]. Independent Component Analysis (ICA) splits independent sound sources to clarify signals, improving the quality of lung sound representations [33]. All these preprocessing techniques adjust features to lift the performance level for machine learning models to ensure strong respiratory sound classification. 

The principles behind the classification of respiratory signals enhance or predispose the grounds for advanced engineering processing methods.

documents.title: Time-Localized Parametric Decomposition of Respiratory Airflow for Sub-Breath Analysis
documents.snippet:
Both discrete and continuous wavelet transforms have been used to extract multiscale features for respiratory event detection [30], [31]. Wavelet coefficients provide a joint time-scale representation that captures irregularities and asymmetries across multiple resolutions, supporting robust classification when combined with oximetry or pressure data [32], [33]. However, the resulting coefficients represent distributions of signal energy rather than explicit waveform components, which makes it difficult to interpret them in terms of physiological events or parameters such as amplitude, onset, or duration [34], [35]. Wavelet-based approaches have been extensively applied for respiratory sound classification [36], [37], demonstrating their utility for energybased feature extraction, though the resulting representations remain challenging to interpret in terms of specific temporal events within individual breaths. 

Data-Driven and Dictionary-Based Approaches. Beyond analytic transforms, adaptive methods such as Matching Pursuit (MP) and K-SVD decompositions have been applied to other biosignals but only rarely to airflow [38]. These techniques reconstruct a signal by selecting or learning atoms from a dictionary, enabling flexible representation of transient patterns. In practice, however, the learned or chosen atoms describe statistical structure in the data and are not explicitly constrained by physiological or morphological models of breathing. Related approaches using empirical mode decomposition (EMD) have been applied to respiratory signals to isolate dominant oscillatory components [39], [40]. EMD and ensemble EMD (EEMD) have been used to extract respiratory rate from photoplethysmographic signals [41], [42] and to differentiate normal from adventitious respiratory sounds [43]. While these decompositions provide adaptive flexibility, the resulting intrinsic modes vary in frequency and phase across realizations, making cross-subject or cross-condition interpre-tation challenging. Moreover, as demonstrated in [37], hybrid approaches combining EMD with continuous wavelet transforms still produce scalogram-based energy representations rather than explicit temporal parameters. 

Morphological Analysis of Airflow Waveforms. Several studies have sought to characterize the overall morphology of the instantaneous airflow waveform using frequency-domain descriptors [16], [17], [18].

documents.title: Novel approach to continuous adventitious respiratory sound analysis for the assessment of bronchodilator response
documents.snippet:
Segmentation of respiratory phases and definition of flow quartiles. The respiratory phases were segmented by means of a zero-crossing detector applied to the flow signals, as described in our previous work [37]. After segmenting the respiratory phases from a subject's three pre-bronchodilator and three post-bronchodilator flow signals, the inspiratory and expiratory flow ranges were calculated as the differences between the maximum and minimum peak flows of all the inspiratory and expiratory phases, respectively. Flow ranges were divided into four quartiles, Q1-Q4, with Q1 including the lowest flows. In this way, a flow quartile was assigned to each respiratory phase, according to its peak flow (Fig 2). 

Acoustic component segmentation and characterization. After having segmented all the respiratory phases, the corresponding respiratory sound signals from the four recorded channels of a subject were analyzed, for acoustic component segmentation, using a new method that we have recently described in two previous studies, based on the analysis of the instantaneous frequency (IF) and envelope (IE) sequences [33], and the Hilbert spectrum time-frequency distribution [34]. The method is briefly described in this section. 

First, our automatic CAS detection algorithm [33] was applied to each respiratory sound signal. Based on the fact that the IF dispersion markedly decreases when CAS appear within a respiratory sound signal, that algorithm detected respiratory sound signal segments that were more likely to contain CAS. To do that, each respiratory sound signal was decomposed by ensemble empirical mode decomposition into a set of narrowband components for which the IF and IE sequences were calculated by means of the Hilbert transform. Then, a number of dispersion-based criteria were used on the IF sequences to detect respiratory sound signal segments with a lower IF dispersion. Each detected segment was characterized by means of a set of features extracted from the IF and IE sequences, including the mean and standard deviation IF. These features were used to classify respiratory sound signal segments as CAS segments or normal segments, using a support vector machine classifier. 

After detecting CAS and normal segments within a respiratory sound signal, the acoustic component segmentation was performed [34].

documents.title: Construction and Validation of an Automatic Segmentation Method for Respiratory Sound Time Labels
documents.snippet:
The rapid development of artificial intelligence enables the identification of previously undetectable patterns in medical imaging and signal data, thereby improving the diagnosis of lung diseases [4][5][6]. Several algorithms have been validated for the robust automation capabilities in the segmentation of respiratory sounds. For example, Huang et al. proposed a technique for the detection and classification of respiratory sounds using vesicular sounds and crackle peak detection [7]. Through quantitative analysis of respiratory sounds, clinicians can differentiate between different types of moist rales, determine their timing within the breathing cycle, and assess their severity. The study conducted by Huang et al. employed an artificial intelligence in terms of deep learning methodology to transform lung sounds into two-dimensional spectrograms and used convolutional neural networks (CNN) for end-to-end recognition of respiratory system diseases or abnormal lung sounds [8]. To achieve segmentation results that align with the sequential nature of respiratory sounds, the author proposes a Python Package called TSSEARCH, which integrates subsequence search and time series similarity measurement with sequence timing models [9]. 

The collected respiratory sounds can be objectively analyzed through computerized intelligent analysis, allowing the signals to be decomposed into different intensities and frequencies for a more accurate characterization of such signals. This technology enables a more objective analysis of respiratory sounds and noise to better understand them [10]. Techniques used in other applications include the determination of breath sound boundaries, feature extraction of breath sounds and noise, differentiation between expiratory and inspiratory phases, and reduction of noise interference. To characterize breath sound parameters in a more accurate way, artificial intelligence algorithms will provide a more intelligent approach used in the overall deciphering process. 

Complex network analysis can be applied to the study of bioacoustics signals and bronchial breath sounds. By utilizing machine learning techniques that extract graph features, the intensity and frequency of respiratory sounds can be measured, which represent fundamental characteristics of sound during the breathing process [11]. In addition, the electronic stethoscope was used to digitize respiratory sounds with full patient cooperation in a quiet environment, while providing hardware and software tools to analyze the raw data. 

The present study introduced a novel approach for the automated segmentation of respiratory sounds and extraction of fundamental frequency and intensity parameters.

Title: Automated Quantitative Analysis of Capnogram Shape for COPD–Normal and COPD–CHF Classification
Snippet: We develop an approach to quantitative analysis of carbon dioxide concentration in exhaled breath, recorded as a function of time by capnography. The generated waveform-or capnogram-is currently used in clinical practice to establish the presence of respiration as well as determine respiratory rate and end-tidal CO2 concentration. The capnogram shape also has diagnostic value, but is presently assessed qualitatively, by visual inspection. Prior approaches to quantitatively characterizing the capnogram shape have explored the correlation of various geometric parameters with pulmonary function tests. These studies attempted to characterize the capnogram in normal subjects and patients with cardiopulmonary disease, but no consistent progress was made, and no translation into clinical practice was achieved. We apply automated quantitative analysis to discriminate between chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and congestive heart failure (CHF), and between COPD and normal. Capnograms were collected from 30 normal subjects, 56 COPD patients, and 53 CHF patients. We computationally extract four physiologically based capnogram features. Classification on a hold-out test set was performed by an ensemble of classifiers employing quadratic discriminant analysis, designed through cross validation on a labeled training set. Using 80 exhalations of each capnogram record in the test set, performance analysis with bootstrapping yields areas under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of 0.89 (95% CI: 0.72-0.96) for COPD/CHF classification, and 0.98 (95% CI: 0.82-1.0) for COPD/normal classification. This classification performance is obtained with a run time sufficiently fast for realtime monitoring.

Title: A machine learning algorithm for detecting abnormal patterns in continuous capnography and pulse oximetry monitoring
Snippet: Opioids are powerful painkillers which are often prescribed after surgery to treat severe pain. However, they come with several adverse effects such as Opioid-Induced Respiratory Depression (OIRD) [2][3][4]. OIRD can lead to severe and to catch true occurrences of respiratory depression without triggering false alarms. 

Continuous capnography and pulse oximetry tracings are affected by many patient-related factors, such as coughing, talking, moving, or equipment-related factors, such as sensor-or calibration errors. Furthermore, there is individual variability in both normal respiratory patterns and the patterns that may indicate respiratory depression. To create an effective alarm system, it is necessary to develop an algorithm that can interpret continuous data, filter out noise, recognize relevant patterns, and make reliable predictions of true events. With the rise of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI), the possibilities to accurately analyze capnography data have increased, yet we are still dealing with the challenge of imbalanced datasets, as explained below. True respiratory depression events are infrequent, as they represent irregularities in a generally regular breathing pattern. Normal breathing patterns are much more common than true respiratory depressions. This leads to an inherent class imbalance in the data. This imbalance can bias ML models towards the majority class, resulting in increased misclassifications. Therefore, solving these challenges is key to improving classification of continuous respiratory measurements. 

Time series classification (TSC) using a multi-stage approach offers a potential solution to the problem of imbalanced data sets. By initially focusing on the separation of normal breathing and abnormal patterns, we can remedy the class imbalance problem. Following initial classification, more complex models may be applied to the refined 'abnormal' dataset in a second stage of the analysis. This sequential method is known to enhance accuracy in anomaly detection and to improve computational efficiency [12,13]. This makes multi-stage TSC a practical and effective strategy for the classification of continuous capnography and pulse oximetry measurements. 

With this approach, the first stage model plays a vital role. The goal of this study is to determine the performance of such a first-stage TSC model.

Title: An Effective Machine Learning Approach for Classifying Artefact-Free and Distorted Capnogram Segments Using Simple Time-Domain Features
Snippet: Capnogram signal analysis has received considerable attention owing to its important applications in assessing cardiopulmonary functions. However, the automatic elimination of deformed parts of a capnogram waveform remains an open research problem. Herein, we introduce an automatic classification approach for discriminating artefact-free (regular) and distorted (irregular) segments of capnogram signals. The proposed features include Hjorth parameters and mean absolute deviation (MAD). The main advantage of these features is their simplicity, such that they can be employed in a computationally efficient machine learning algorithm. MATLAB simulation is conducted on 100 regular and 100 irregular segments of capnogram to extract the proposed and existing features, which are ranked based on the Pearson correlation coefficient, ${p}$ -value and area under receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. The naive Bayes, decision tree, random forest and support vector machine (SVM) classifiers are fed by the relatively highly ranked features, and the classification performance is assessed via ten-fold cross-validation. Besides the linear kernel SVM, the radial basis function (RBF) and polynomial kernel functions with different orders are also included in the current experiment. Results revealed the effectiveness of the Hjorth activity and MAD attributes when used with the fourth-order polynomial kernel-SVM classifier. The achieved accuracy, precision and specificity are 89%, 92.1%, and 91% outperforming the existing method by 2.5%, 5.6% and 7%, respectively. The simplicity of the proposed time-domain features is confirmed by the average total computational time of features extraction and classification phases which is only 13 ms instead of 19 ms in the case of incorporating both time- and frequency-domain features, indicating a reduction of 31.6%. It is envisaged that the proposed approach can be valuable if implemented with capnography devices for real-time and fully automated capnogram-based respiratory assessment. Even so, further research is recommended to enhance the classification performance through exploring more features and/or classifiers.

Herein, we introduce an automatic classification approach for discriminating artefact-free (regular) and distorted (irregular) segments of capnogram signals. The proposed features include Hjorth parameters and mean absolute deviation (MAD). The main advantage of these features is their simplicity, such that they can be employed in a computationally efficient machine learning algorithm. MATLAB simulation is conducted on 100 regular and 100 irregular segments of capnogram to extract the proposed and existing features, which are ranked based on the Pearson correlation coefficient, ${p}$ -value and area under receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. The naive Bayes, decision tree, random forest and support vector machine (SVM) classifiers are fed by the relatively highly ranked features, and the classification performance is assessed via ten-fold cross-validation. Besides the linear kernel SVM, the radial basis function (RBF) and polynomial kernel functions with different orders are also included in the current experiment. Results revealed the effectiveness of the Hjorth activity and MAD attributes when used with the fourth-order polynomial kernel-SVM classifier. The achieved accuracy, precision and specificity are 89%, 92.1%, and 91% outperforming the existing method by 2.5%, 5.6% and 7%, respectively. The simplicity of the proposed time-domain features is confirmed by the average total computational time of features extraction and classification phases which is only 13 ms instead of 19 ms in the case of incorporating both time- and frequency-domain features, indicating a reduction of 31.6%. It is envisaged that the proposed approach can be valuable if implemented with capnography devices for real-time and fully automated capnogram-based respiratory assessment. Even so, further research is recommended to enhance the classification performance through exploring more features and/or classifiers.

documents.title: An Effective Machine Learning Approach for Classifying Artefact-Free and Distorted Capnogram Segments Using Simple Time-Domain Features

Even though selecting the regular capnogram segments and discarding the irregular ones is an essential prerequisite for capnogram-based lung diseases detection and classification, the automatization of this step using machine learning techniques has not yet received the attention it deserves in the literature. That being the case, the present study is mainly concerned with bridging this research gap. 

The rest of the article is organized as follows. Section II discusses the previous related work. Section III presents the material and methods in which the existing and proposed features as well as the employed classifier and features ranking metrics are explained. Section IV includes the results and discussion. Finally, Section V concludes the paper.

harder.brainstorming: The seed is a straightforward methods survey: retrieve breath-analysis papers and list pattern-detection techniques. One option is to ask about choosing between methods, but comparative studies may directly state when to use each. A stronger option exploits that the question implicitly assumes patterns ARE present and worth finding—but for some breath measurements (especially in uncontrolled settings or certain populations), published literature shows that apparent patterns are artifacts of confounds like mouth-breathing, ambient conditions, or sensor drift rather than meaningful physiological signals.
harder.chosen_strategy: Require recognition of an implicit false premise: challenge the assumption that detected patterns in breath data are necessarily meaningful rather than artifacts of measurement confounds.
harder.updated_question: How can I find meaningful physiological patterns in breath data rather than measurement artifacts?
harder.why_harder: A system can easily retrieve pattern-detection methods from breath-analysis literature, but answering THIS question requires recognizing that many published 'patterns' are later shown to be confounds (e.g., mouth-breathing contamination, humidity effects, sensor baseline drift, body position changes). The system must synthesize across methodological critiques that explain why initial pattern claims failed to replicate, rather than simply cataloging successful pattern-finding techniques. This requires evaluating validity of patterns, not just detecting them.
harder.verification_criterion: The answer must explicitly warn that breath measurements are susceptible to at least two specific artifact sources (e.g., mouth-breathing, ambient humidity/temperature, sensor drift, body position, circadian variation) that can produce spurious patterns, AND propose at least one concrete methodological control for distinguishing artifacts from physiological signals (e.g., controlling for ambient conditions, comparing nose-only vs mouth-breathing, using drift-correction algorithms, or validating against known physiological ground truth). Fails if it only lists pattern-detection algorithms without addressing artifact identification, or if it treats all detected patterns as equally valid without discussing confound mitigation.

Below is a practical, evidence‑backed workflow to extract meaningful physiological breathing patterns while minimizing measurement artifacts. It combines sensor‑level checks, preprocessing pipelines tuned to respiratory dynamics, cross‑channel validation, and study‑level design choices that help distinguish true respiratory physiology from artifacts.

1) Principles: separate respiratory oscillations from drift, noise, and motion
- Respiratory signals are dominated by oscillations in the 0.05–0.5 Hz (10–60 breaths/min) band, with useful details across 0.05–1 Hz for slow breathing; preprocessing should remove low‑frequency baseline wander and high‑frequency noise while preserving the respiratory waveform phase and pulse-related features. <cite id="e3439438-1">Baseline wander in respiratory recordings arises from muscle movement or posture changes and is commonly addressed by low‑pass filtering and detrending; normalization improves consistency for downstream analysis</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-0">Effective stacks combine temporal smoothing (e.g., Savitzky–Golay), DC removal (mean subtraction), variance normalization, and two‑stage bandpass filtering (e.g., second‑order Butterworth) with zero‑phase forward–backward filtering to preserve temporal structure for accurate rate detection</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-2">Detrending and bandpass filtering in the 0.1–0.6 Hz range has been used to isolate respiration‑dominant oscillations, suppressing illumination variation, motion artifacts, and slow drift</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-3">Two‑step pipelines (moving average baseline removal then lowpass) tuned to [0.066–0.917 Hz] effectively target normal breathing rates</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">After artifact cleaning (including handling invalid/abnormal values, drift, and high‑frequency spikes), low‑pass, moving‑average, and Savitzky–Golay filters (including pre‑derivatives) reveal true desaturation and airflow patterns while preserving clinically relevant events</cite>.

2) Common artifact sources in breath signals and how to detect/mitigate them
- Flow/pressure sensors: pneumotachograph condensation and leaks
  - Condensation increases differential pressure nonlinearity and drifts flow/volume over time, inflating measured tidal volume and distorting waveforms; periodic calibration and thermal conditioning/drainage are needed. <cite id="e47c1715-0">In an infant ventilator simulation, two of three pneumotachograph flow sensors showed stepwise increases of 0.5 mL then 4 mL tidal volume over two hours, while one maintained stability; condensation in pneumotachographs can therefore yield falsely high tidal volumes</cite>. 
  - Mechanical ventilation: reference volume location matters; taking inspiration‑limb output as the reference overestimates tidal volume in leaks, whereas expiratory‑limb references avoid this but can be impacted by expiratory leaks in the opposite direction. <cite id="e47c1715-3">Reference volumes on the inspiratory limb can be overestimated with leaks, prompting inappropriate pressure reductions; expiratory‑limb references avoid this leak bias on inspiration but may underestimate with expiratory leaks</cite>. 
  - Practical robustness: low‑cost pneumotachographs can perform acceptably when carefully built and calibrated; errors near 2–4% of VT can be achieved for typical tidal volumes, comparable to well‑serviced ICU ventilators. <cite id="e47c1715-1">Low‑cost pneumotachographs constructed by drilled‑hole plates and calibrated via simple resuscitation bag maneuvers achieved VT errors of 2.1% on average and <4% worst case under realistic ventilation settings</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-2">Repeated calibration maneuvers (averaging K1, K2) reduced variance in tidal volume computation; typical errors were within accepted tolerances (e.g., ±(4.0 mL + 15% of volume)), and observed errors were often lower than required clinical precision windows</cite>. 
- Forced oscillation/spirometry artifacts: occlusion, leak, drift, and glottal closure invalidate breaths; acceptability criteria and exclusions help avoid artifact‑contaminated segments. <cite id="8bb205ae-0">Standard FOT/flow procedures accept trials only when at least three breaths are free from occlusion, leak, or drift, and exclude extreme/negative resistance events</cite>. <cite id="8bb205ae-2">IOS measurements during tidal breathing require trials without glottis closure and mouth leak; otherwise data are excluded</cite>.
- Motion/illumination and coupling artifacts in noncontact/video or remote sensing
  - Motion can couple to optical/PPG signals; mitigations include dual‑ROI tracking, motion‑robust smoothing/derivative preprocessing, and cross‑sensor validation against spirometry. <cite id="e3439438-0">Temporal smoothing and DC removal combined with bandpass filtering isolate respiratory components and minimize artifacts for noncontact motion‑derived signals</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-3">For textile inductive respiratory sensors, a 4‑s moving‑average detrending followed by 0.917 Hz lowpass (bi‑directional) suppresses drift and high‑frequency motion while targeting normal breathing frequencies</cite>. <cite id="8bb205ae-3">Motion artifacts in PPG/remote video are common; specific motion‑aware ROI tracking reduces artifacts in tidal volume estimation, but methods differ from regular PPG and do not capture forward–backward trunk motion</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Savitzky–Golay filtering before computing derivatives and replacing impossible/invalid values improves robustness of airflow/SpO2 features to motion and spikes</cite>.
- Power line and physiological coupling: use notch filters and cross‑correlation checks
  - Physiological and technical oscillations (cardiac pulse, 50/60 Hz power line) can modulate respiratory signals; artifact‑aware analysis tools provide options to remove baseline drift, notch 50 Hz, and choose low‑pass cut‑offs, and to separate respiratory vs cardiac patterns. <cite id="e3439438-0">Zero‑phase Butterworth bandpass selection aligned with respiratory bands suppresses power‑line and high‑frequency confounders while preserving respiratory frequency content</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Lowpass and moving‑average smoothing reduce high‑frequency spikes that can mimic slow respiratory changes</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-4">Toolchains (e.g., NICA) allow selecting artifact removal models to remove pulsation of the heart and baseline drift, and apply notch and low‑pass filters to remove technical artifacts</cite>.

3) Algorithmic pipeline: from raw breath data to physiologically interpretable patterns
- Preprocessing to remove artifacts and center dynamics
  - Smooth with Savitzky–Golay to preserve waveform features while cutting noise; subtract moving average/DC to remove baseline wander; normalize to unit variance for consistency; high‑pass/low‑pass to define respiratory band; apply forward–backward (zero‑phase) filtering to preserve timing for rate/phase features. <cite id="e3439438-0">Savitzky–Golay smoothing with mean subtraction (DC removal), variance normalization, and two‑stage bandpass filtering yields a clean respiratory signal suitable for further analysis</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-2">Detrending and 0.1–0.6 Hz bandpass filtering remove illumination/motion drifts and preserve respiration‑dominant oscillations</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-3">Moving‑average detrending then 0.917 Hz lowpass targets normal breathing ranges</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Handling invalid/physically impossible values, smoothing extreme spikes, and drift correction in airflow/SpO2 ensure physiologically meaningful patterns remain for features</cite>.
- Feature extraction aligned to physiology
  - Respiratory rate and tidal volume: spectral peaks near 0.2–0.3 Hz, waveform skew/phase, and derivative‑based volume from flow; windowing aligns local events (onset, flow limitation, desaturation). <cite id="e3439438-0">Bandpass and smoothing preserve pulse‑related components enabling accurate rate estimation</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-2">After detrend/bandpass, signals support spectral analysis of respiratory oscillations</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Windowing airflow and SpO2 into short fixed‑length segments enables learning local temporal patterns such as apnea onset, airflow reduction, and oxygen decline</cite>.
- Cross‑channel validation to separate cardiac vs respiratory modulation
  - Cross‑correlate respiratory features with ECG/PPG respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) and heart period; use bandpass‑limited respiratory signals to capture cardiac coupling within normal RSA ranges rather than over‑interpreting high‑frequency phasic oscillations. <cite id="e3439438-0">Maintaining phase integrity during bandpass filtering is critical for reliable frequency estimation and RR detection, enabling clear separation of respiratory modulation from high‑frequency noise</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Savitzky–Golay smoothing before derivatives and lowpass filtering help reveal true desaturation patterns and airflow changes without distorting clinically relevant events</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-4">Artifact removal models that remove cardiac pulsation and baseline drift, combined with notch/low‑pass filters, allow isolating respiratory patterns from heart and technical artifacts in near‑infrared/PPG‑adjacent workflows</cite>.
- Handling noninvasive ventilator contexts
  - In volume‑assured modes, prefer expiratory‑limb reference volumes to avoid inspiration‑limb leak overestimation; continuously monitor for expiratory leaks; apply equalization delays to account for transport delays; incorporate pneumotachograph maintenance (drainage/condensate management) into protocols. <cite id="e47c1715-3">Using expiratory‑limb reference volumes avoids inspiration‑limb leak overestimation, though expiratory leaks can still bias VT if sampled there</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-0">Condensation increases differential pressure and biases tidal volume upward over time; regular monitoring shows measurable drift within hours</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-1">Simple pneumotachographs, when built and calibrated per procedure, accurately measure inspiratory flow and VT comparable to ICU standards</cite>.
- Mask fit and airway resistance artifacts in spirometry/IOS
  - Exclude breaths with occlusion, mouth leak, or glottal closure; ensure proper nose clips and cheek support; recognize that subtle small‑airway dysfunction can manifest as expiratory flow limitation and reduced mid‑expiratory flow. <cite id="8bb205ae-0">Breath acceptability criteria exclude occlusion/leak/drift and extreme/negative resistance</cite>. <cite id="8bb205ae-2">Leak and glottis closure events are explicitly excluded to avoid biasing resistance/reactance derivations</cite>. <cite id="8bb205ae-1">During IOS on tidal breathing, proper technique (nose clip, cheek support) and analysis of R5, X5, ΔR5–20, and AX are used; airflow limitation on expiration is visually identifiable</cite>.

4) Validation strategies: artifact robustness and clinical plausibility
- Trial/segment acceptability and repeatability: apply per‑trial quality checks (no occlusion/leak/drift), and require multiple acceptable breaths per measurement; compute mean across acceptable trials to reduce single‑event artifacts. <cite id="8bb205ae-0">Acceptability requires at least three artifact‑free breaths; extreme/negative resistance breaths are excluded</cite>. <cite id="8bb205ae-2">Trials with glottis closure and mouth leak are excluded from analysis</cite>.
- Cross‑sensor triangulation: align noncontact/inductive/PPG‑derived respiratory features with reference spirometry/SpO2; if trends diverge by >10–20% or show systematic phase bias, revisit sensor placement, leak, or preprocessing. <cite id="e3439438-0">Noncontact pipelines that preserve phase and respiratory spectral features have yielded signals suitable for accurate RR detection and can be cross‑validated against other modalities</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Resampling and cleaning pipelines for SpO2 and airflow reveal true desaturation and airflow events and enable direct cross‑channel comparisons</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-1">Low‑cost pneumotachographs aligned to reference devices showed VT errors near 2–4%, supporting cross‑sensor calibration and validation</cite>.
- Baseline and drift checks: plot rolling means/variances over time, examine spectral power near 0.05–0.6 Hz, and compare against expected breathing rate distributions; flag segments with drift >few percent per minute or spectral contamination near 50/60 Hz as artifact. <cite id="e3439438-0">DC removal and bandpass confine drift and noise outside the respiratory band, enabling artifact‑free spectral analysis</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Replacing impossible values, smoothing spikes, and drift correction specifically target drift/power artifacts in airflow/SpO2</cite>.
- Surrogate/benchmark tests: compare processed signals to artifact‑matched surrogates (e.g., phase‑randomized respiratory waveforms within bandpass limits) to ensure detected rhythms are not dominated by noise or cardiac modulation; compare cross‑correlation magnitudes with ECG to bound RSA contributions. <cite id="e3439438-0">Phase‑preserving filtering enables reliable frequency/RR estimation; absence of high‑frequency artifacts reduces risk of spurious oscillations</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-4">Artifact removal models that remove cardiac pulsation and baseline drift provide a principled way to construct physiological surrogate baselines for comparison</cite>.
- Clinical pattern plausibility: screen for known pathophysiologies that reshape breathing patterns (e.g., obstructive flow limitation, periodic expiratory flow limitation in sleep apnea, shallow/rapid breathing in anxiety, prolonged expiratory time in COPD) and incorporate domain checks (e.g., flow‑limitation detection, expiratory time > 4 s). <cite id="8bb205ae-1">Oscillometry/IOS on tidal breathing highlights frequency‑dependent resistance and reactance indices; visually identified tidal flow limitation superimposed on maximal flow aids small airway dysfunction assessment</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Windowed SpO2 and airflow features capture apnea onset and airflow reduction patterns, supporting sleep‑disordered breathing detection</cite>.

5) Practical workflow checklist
- Sensor setup and calibration
  - For pneumotachographs: ensure dry operation (heaters/drainage) or monitor condensate; swap to output limb reference for volume‑assured modes to avoid inspiratory leak bias; if using low‑cost builds, perform two‑maneuver calibration and repeat to average K1/K2; maintain tolerance within ±(4 mL + 15% of VT). <cite id="e47c1715-0">Condensation can bias VT upward within hours; monitor drift</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-3">Inspiration‑limb reference overestimates VT with leaks; expiratory‑limb reference avoids this but can be biased by expiratory leaks</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-1">Low‑cost pneumotachographs with proper calibration match reference devices with VT errors near 2–4%</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-2">Repeat two‑maneuver calibration improves robust K1/K2 and reduces VT variance</cite>.
- Data acquisition hygiene
  - Record high‑quality metadata (sampling rate, zeroing, baseline offset); screen for invalid/clip values; enforce artifact‑free trials (no occlusion/leak/drift, no glottal closure); exclude breaths with mouth leak or valve chatter. <cite id="8bb205ae-0">Acceptability excludes occlusion/leak/drift and extreme resistance; at least three artifact‑free breaths required</cite>. <cite id="8bb205ae-2">Trials with glottis closure and mouth leak are explicitly excluded</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Replace impossible values, smooth spikes, and correct drift in airflow signals</cite>.
- Preprocessing to isolate physiology
  - Apply Savitzky–Golay smoothing; subtract moving average/DC; normalize variance; apply zero‑phase bandpass (e.g., 0.05–0.6 Hz) and compute derivatives after smoothing; remove outliers and short gaps with interpolation or replacement. <cite id="e3439438-0">Savitzky–Golay smoothing, DC removal, normalization, and bandpass with zero‑phase filtering preserve respiratory features for RR detection</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-2">Detrend + 0.1–0.6 Hz bandpass isolates respiration‑dominant oscillations</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-3">4‑s moving‑average detrending then 0.917 Hz lowpass targets 4–55 rpm</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Savitzky–Golay before derivatives and outlier replacement/interpolation preserve events while suppressing spikes</cite>.
- Cross‑channel validation and artifact separation
  - Cross‑correlate respiratory signals with ECG/PPG to quantify cardiac coupling; if cross‑correlation peaks at cardiac (0–0.15 Hz) rather than respiratory (0.15–0.5 Hz) bands, reassign phasic components or mask cardiac beats; use notch 50/60 Hz and baseline drift removal to limit technical coupling. <cite id="e3439438-0">Phase‑preserving filtering supports accurate respiratory frequency estimation and separation from high‑frequency noise</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-4">Select artifact removal models to remove pulsation and baseline drift; apply notch and low‑pass filters to exclude technical artifacts</cite>.
- Pattern interpretation and clinical checks
  - Compute RR, tidal volume, minute ventilation, and skew/phase; screen for flow limitation (expiratory decel, superposition on maximal flow), prolonged expiratory time, or irregular cycles; compare to normative IOS/ventilation indices; flag breaths where VT% or AX change exceeds expected physiological variance. <cite id="8bb205ae-1">Normal tidal breathing with IOS yields interpretable R5, X5, ΔR5–20, AX; expiratory flow limitation is visually identifiable on airflow traces</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Windowing reveals apnea onset, airflow reduction, and oxygen decline patterns that align with clinical OSA features</cite>.
- Reproducibility and drift monitoring
  - Re‑calibrate sensors periodically (daily/overnight) and compare baseline drift of processed respiratory signals across runs; if drift exceeds 2–3% per hour or spectral power shifts outside respiratory band, reprocess or re‑acquire. <cite id="e47c1715-0">Condensate‑related drift can increase VT by mL over hours; reprocessing without drift yields more reliable results</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-2">Improved calibration procedures reduce variance in VT and bring errors within accepted tolerances</cite>.

6) When artifacts dominate and how to handle them
- If cleaned respiratory power remains concentrated near 0–0.1 Hz without clinically interpretable oscillations, reassess pneumotachograph leaks, mask/nasal valve tightness, patient effort (agonal index), and motion; add ECG cross‑correlation to exclude cardiac drift dominance. <cite id="e47c1715-0">Condensation and differential pressure drift can inflate VT and distort waveforms</cite>. <cite id="8bb205ae-0">Occlusion/leak/drift invalidate breaths and should be excluded to avoid misleading resistance/oscillation estimates</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Replacing impossible values, correcting drift, and smoothing spikes restore meaningful patterns for features</cite>.
- If noncontact signals show strong motion artifacts, use dual‑ROI or trunk‑based tracking, apply motion‑robust Savitzky–Golay smoothing, and cross‑validate with spirometry; avoid forward–backward filtering if it blurs phase, and prefer bandpass within 0.05–0.5 Hz for slow breathing. <cite id="8bb205ae-3">Motion artifacts in remote respiratory signals require tracking strategies; small ROIs reduce artifacts but miss forward–backward trunk motions</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-0">Phase‑preserving zero‑phase filters are essential when timing matters; smoothing plus DC removal plus bandpass isolates respiratory components from motion</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-3">Lowpass near 0.917 Hz suppresses high‑frequency motion while preserving normal breathing</cite>.
- For ventilated patients, prefer expiratory‑limb volume references, monitor leak continuously, and add transport delay compensation when estimating VT; swap to inspiratory‑limb reference only when expiratory leaks are controlled and confirmed not to bias VT. <cite id="e47c1715-3">Reference placement (inspiratory vs expiratory) has opposite leak biases; choose expiratory to avoid inspiration leak overestimation but watch for expiratory leak underestimation</cite>.

7) Example end‑to‑end pipelines
- Noninvasive monitoring at home
  - Place oximeter on finger, secure chest sensor; record airflow via nasal port; preprocess with Savitzky–Golay(5,2), mean subtraction, variance normalization, bandpass 0.05–0.5 Hz, notch 50 Hz; compute RR and tidal volume from flow integration; cross‑correlate respiratory waveform with PPG to confirm weak cardiac coupling; flag breaths with drift >5% per minute or extreme spikes. <cite id="e3439438-0">Smoothing, DC removal, normalization, and bandpass preserve respiratory features for RR detection</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">PPG/SpO2 artifacts are mitigated via smoothing and drift correction to reveal true desaturation and airflow changes</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-4">Notch and low‑pass filters remove technical artifacts; artifact‑aware models remove pulsation and baseline drift</cite>.
- Sleep lab PSG with home‑portable devices
  - Resample SpO2/flow to 5 Hz to preserve desaturation/flow events while reducing compute; interpolate short gaps, replace impossible values, smooth extreme spikes, and correct airflow baseline drift; window into 30‑s segments for OSA/RERA detection, computing slope and magnitude features of airflow and desaturation. <cite id="e3439438-4">Resampling to 5 Hz preserves desaturation and airflow events; artifact detection and correction (interpolation, value replacement, smoothing, drift correction) leaves physiologically meaningful patterns for features</cite>.
- Clinical spirometry/IOS

  - Condensation increases differential pressure nonlinearity and drifts flow/volume over time, inflating measured tidal volume and distorting waveforms; periodic calibration and thermal conditioning/drainage are needed. <cite id="e47c1715-0">In an infant ventilator simulation, two of three pneumotachograph flow sensors showed stepwise increases of 0.5 mL then 4 mL tidal volume over two hours, while one maintained stability; condensation in pneumotachographs can therefore yield falsely high tidal volumes</cite>.
