  - Practical robustness: low‑cost pneumotachographs can perform acceptably when carefully built and calibrated; errors near 2–4% of VT can be achieved for typical tidal volumes, comparable to well‑serviced ICU ventilators. <cite id="e47c1715-1">Low‑cost pneumotachographs constructed by drilled‑hole plates and calibrated via simple resuscitation bag maneuvers achieved VT errors of 2.1% on average and <4% worst case under realistic ventilation settings</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-2">Repeated calibration maneuvers (averaging K1, K2) reduced variance in tidal volume computation; typical errors were within accepted tolerances (e.g., ±(4.0 mL + 15% of volume)), and observed errors were often lower than required clinical precision windows</cite>. 
- Forced oscillation/spirometry artifacts: occlusion, leak, drift, and glottal closure invalidate breaths; acceptability criteria and exclusions help avoid artifact‑contaminated segments. <cite id="8bb205ae-0">Standard FOT/flow procedures accept trials only when at least three breaths are free from occlusion, leak, or drift, and exclude extreme/negative resistance events</cite>. <cite id="8bb205ae-2">IOS measurements during tidal breathing require trials without glottis closure and mouth leak; otherwise data are excluded</cite>.
- Motion/illumination and coupling artifacts in noncontact/video or remote sensing
  - Motion can couple to optical/PPG signals; mitigations include dual‑ROI tracking, motion‑robust smoothing/derivative preprocessing, and cross‑sensor validation against spirometry. <cite id="e3439438-0">Temporal smoothing and DC removal combined with bandpass filtering isolate respiratory components and minimize artifacts for noncontact motion‑derived signals</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-3">For textile inductive respiratory sensors, a 4‑s moving‑average detrending followed by 0.917 Hz lowpass (bi‑directional) suppresses drift and high‑frequency motion while targeting normal breathing frequencies</cite>. <cite id="8bb205ae-3">Motion artifacts in PPG/remote video are common; specific motion‑aware ROI tracking reduces artifacts in tidal volume estimation, but methods differ from regular PPG and do not capture forward–backward trunk motion</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Savitzky–Golay filtering before computing derivatives and replacing impossible/invalid values improves robustness of airflow/SpO2 features to motion and spikes</cite>.
- Power line and physiological coupling: use notch filters and cross‑correlation checks
  - Physiological and technical oscillations (cardiac pulse, 50/60 Hz power line) can modulate respiratory signals; artifact‑aware analysis tools provide options to remove baseline drift, notch 50 Hz, and choose low‑pass cut‑offs, and to separate respiratory vs cardiac patterns. <cite id="e3439438-0">Zero‑phase Butterworth bandpass selection aligned with respiratory bands suppresses power‑line and high‑frequency confounders while preserving respiratory frequency content</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Lowpass and moving‑average smoothing reduce high‑frequency spikes that can mimic slow respiratory changes</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-4">Toolchains (e.g., NICA) allow selecting artifact removal models to remove pulsation of the heart and baseline drift, and apply notch and low‑pass filters to remove technical artifacts</cite>.

3) Algorithmic pipeline: from raw breath data to physiologically interpretable patterns
- Preprocessing to remove artifacts and center dynamics
  - Smooth with Savitzky–Golay to preserve waveform features while cutting noise; subtract moving average/DC to remove baseline wander; normalize to unit variance for consistency; high‑pass/low‑pass to define respiratory band; apply forward–backward (zero‑phase) filtering to preserve timing for rate/phase features. <cite id="e3439438-0">Savitzky–Golay smoothing with mean subtraction (DC removal), variance normalization, and two‑stage bandpass filtering yields a clean respiratory signal suitable for further analysis</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-2">Detrending and 0.1–0.6 Hz bandpass filtering remove illumination/motion drifts and preserve respiration‑dominant oscillations</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-3">Moving‑average detrending then 0.917 Hz lowpass targets normal breathing ranges</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Handling invalid/physically impossible values, smoothing extreme spikes, and drift correction in airflow/SpO2 ensure physiologically meaningful patterns remain for features</cite>.
- Feature extraction aligned to physiology
  - Respiratory rate and tidal volume: spectral peaks near 0.2–0.3 Hz, waveform skew/phase, and derivative‑based volume from flow; windowing aligns local events (onset, flow limitation, desaturation). <cite id="e3439438-0">Bandpass and smoothing preserve pulse‑related components enabling accurate rate estimation</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-2">After detrend/bandpass, signals support spectral analysis of respiratory oscillations</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Windowing airflow and SpO2 into short fixed‑length segments enables learning local temporal patterns such as apnea onset, airflow reduction, and oxygen decline</cite>.
- Cross‑channel validation to separate cardiac vs respiratory modulation
  - Cross‑correlate respiratory features with ECG/PPG respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) and heart period; use bandpass‑limited respiratory signals to capture cardiac coupling within normal RSA ranges rather than over‑interpreting high‑frequency phasic oscillations. <cite id="e3439438-0">Maintaining phase integrity during bandpass filtering is critical for reliable frequency estimation and RR detection, enabling clear separation of respiratory modulation from high‑frequency noise</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Savitzky–Golay smoothing before derivatives and lowpass filtering help reveal true desaturation patterns and airflow changes without distorting clinically relevant events</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-4">Artifact removal models that remove cardiac pulsation and baseline drift, combined with notch/low‑pass filters, allow isolating respiratory patterns from heart and technical artifacts in near‑infrared/PPG‑adjacent workflows</cite>.
- Handling noninvasive ventilator contexts
  - In volume‑assured modes, prefer expiratory‑limb reference volumes to avoid inspiration‑limb leak overestimation; continuously monitor for expiratory leaks; apply equalization delays to account for transport delays; incorporate pneumotachograph maintenance (drainage/condensate management) into protocols. <cite id="e47c1715-3">Using expiratory‑limb reference volumes avoids inspiration‑limb leak overestimation, though expiratory leaks can still bias VT if sampled there</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-0">Condensation increases differential pressure and biases tidal volume upward over time; regular monitoring shows measurable drift within hours</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-1">Simple pneumotachographs, when built and calibrated per procedure, accurately measure inspiratory flow and VT comparable to ICU standards</cite>.
- Mask fit and airway resistance artifacts in spirometry/IOS
  - Exclude breaths with occlusion, mouth leak, or glottal closure; ensure proper nose clips and cheek support; recognize that subtle small‑airway dysfunction can manifest as expiratory flow limitation and reduced mid‑expiratory flow. <cite id="8bb205ae-0">Breath acceptability criteria exclude occlusion/leak/drift and extreme/negative resistance</cite>. <cite id="8bb205ae-2">Leak and glottis closure events are explicitly excluded to avoid biasing resistance/reactance derivations</cite>. <cite id="8bb205ae-1">During IOS on tidal breathing, proper technique (nose clip, cheek support) and analysis of R5, X5, ΔR5–20, and AX are used; airflow limitation on expiration is visually identifiable</cite>.

4) Validation strategies: artifact robustness and clinical plausibility
- Trial/segment acceptability and repeatability: apply per‑trial quality checks (no occlusion/leak/drift), and require multiple acceptable breaths per measurement; compute mean across acceptable trials to reduce single‑event artifacts. <cite id="8bb205ae-0">Acceptability requires at least three artifact‑free breaths; extreme/negative resistance breaths are excluded</cite>. <cite id="8bb205ae-2">Trials with glottis closure and mouth leak are excluded from analysis</cite>.
- Cross‑sensor triangulation: align noncontact/inductive/PPG‑derived respiratory features with reference spirometry/SpO2; if trends diverge by >10–20% or show systematic phase bias, revisit sensor placement, leak, or preprocessing. <cite id="e3439438-0">Noncontact pipelines that preserve phase and respiratory spectral features have yielded signals suitable for accurate RR detection and can be cross‑validated against other modalities</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Resampling and cleaning pipelines for SpO2 and airflow reveal true desaturation and airflow events and enable direct cross‑channel comparisons</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-1">Low‑cost pneumotachographs aligned to reference devices showed VT errors near 2–4%, supporting cross‑sensor calibration and validation</cite>.
- Baseline and drift checks: plot rolling means/variances over time, examine spectral power near 0.05–0.6 Hz, and compare against expected breathing rate distributions; flag segments with drift >few percent per minute or spectral contamination near 50/60 Hz as artifact. <cite id="e3439438-0">DC removal and bandpass confine drift and noise outside the respiratory band, enabling artifact‑free spectral analysis</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Replacing impossible values, smoothing spikes, and drift correction specifically target drift/power artifacts in airflow/SpO2</cite>.
- Surrogate/benchmark tests: compare processed signals to artifact‑matched surrogates (e.g., phase‑randomized respiratory waveforms within bandpass limits) to ensure detected rhythms are not dominated by noise or cardiac modulation; compare cross‑correlation magnitudes with ECG to bound RSA contributions. <cite id="e3439438-0">Phase‑preserving filtering enables reliable frequency/RR estimation; absence of high‑frequency artifacts reduces risk of spurious oscillations</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-4">Artifact removal models that remove cardiac pulsation and baseline drift provide a principled way to construct physiological surrogate baselines for comparison</cite>.
- Clinical pattern plausibility: screen for known pathophysiologies that reshape breathing patterns (e.g., obstructive flow limitation, periodic expiratory flow limitation in sleep apnea, shallow/rapid breathing in anxiety, prolonged expiratory time in COPD) and incorporate domain checks (e.g., flow‑limitation detection, expiratory time > 4 s). <cite id="8bb205ae-1">Oscillometry/IOS on tidal breathing highlights frequency‑dependent resistance and reactance indices; visually identified tidal flow limitation superimposed on maximal flow aids small airway dysfunction assessment</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Windowed SpO2 and airflow features capture apnea onset and airflow reduction patterns, supporting sleep‑disordered breathing detection</cite>.

5) Practical workflow checklist
- Sensor setup and calibration
  - For pneumotachographs: ensure dry operation (heaters/drainage) or monitor condensate; swap to output limb reference for volume‑assured modes to avoid inspiratory leak bias; if using low‑cost builds, perform two‑maneuver calibration and repeat to average K1/K2; maintain tolerance within ±(4 mL + 15% of VT). <cite id="e47c1715-0">Condensation can bias VT upward within hours; monitor drift</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-3">Inspiration‑limb reference overestimates VT with leaks; expiratory‑limb reference avoids this but can be biased by expiratory leaks</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-1">Low‑cost pneumotachographs with proper calibration match reference devices with VT errors near 2–4%</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-2">Repeat two‑maneuver calibration improves robust K1/K2 and reduces VT variance</cite>.
- Data acquisition hygiene
  - Record high‑quality metadata (sampling rate, zeroing, baseline offset); screen for invalid/clip values; enforce artifact‑free trials (no occlusion/leak/drift, no glottal closure); exclude breaths with mouth leak or valve chatter. <cite id="8bb205ae-0">Acceptability excludes occlusion/leak/drift and extreme resistance; at least three artifact‑free breaths required</cite>. <cite id="8bb205ae-2">Trials with glottis closure and mouth leak are explicitly excluded</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Replace impossible values, smooth spikes, and correct drift in airflow signals</cite>.
- Preprocessing to isolate physiology
  - Apply Savitzky–Golay smoothing; subtract moving average/DC; normalize variance; apply zero‑phase bandpass (e.g., 0.05–0.6 Hz) and compute derivatives after smoothing; remove outliers and short gaps with interpolation or replacement. <cite id="e3439438-0">Savitzky–Golay smoothing, DC removal, normalization, and bandpass with zero‑phase filtering preserve respiratory features for RR detection</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-2">Detrend + 0.1–0.6 Hz bandpass isolates respiration‑dominant oscillations</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-3">4‑s moving‑average detrending then 0.917 Hz lowpass targets 4–55 rpm</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Savitzky–Golay before derivatives and outlier replacement/interpolation preserve events while suppressing spikes</cite>.
- Cross‑channel validation and artifact separation
  - Cross‑correlate respiratory signals with ECG/PPG to quantify cardiac coupling; if cross‑correlation peaks at cardiac (0–0.15 Hz) rather than respiratory (0.15–0.5 Hz) bands, reassign phasic components or mask cardiac beats; use notch 50/60 Hz and baseline drift removal to limit technical coupling. <cite id="e3439438-0">Phase‑preserving filtering supports accurate respiratory frequency estimation and separation from high‑frequency noise</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-4">Select artifact removal models to remove pulsation and baseline drift; apply notch and low‑pass filters to exclude technical artifacts</cite>.
- Pattern interpretation and clinical checks
  - Compute RR, tidal volume, minute ventilation, and skew/phase; screen for flow limitation (expiratory decel, superposition on maximal flow), prolonged expiratory time, or irregular cycles; compare to normative IOS/ventilation indices; flag breaths where VT% or AX change exceeds expected physiological variance. <cite id="8bb205ae-1">Normal tidal breathing with IOS yields interpretable R5, X5, ΔR5–20, AX; expiratory flow limitation is visually identifiable on airflow traces</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Windowing reveals apnea onset, airflow reduction, and oxygen decline patterns that align with clinical OSA features</cite>.
- Reproducibility and drift monitoring
  - Re‑calibrate sensors periodically (daily/overnight) and compare baseline drift of processed respiratory signals across runs; if drift exceeds 2–3% per hour or spectral power shifts outside respiratory band, reprocess or re‑acquire. <cite id="e47c1715-0">Condensate‑related drift can increase VT by mL over hours; reprocessing without drift yields more reliable results</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-2">Improved calibration procedures reduce variance in VT and bring errors within accepted tolerances</cite>.

6) When artifacts dominate and how to handle them
- If cleaned respiratory power remains concentrated near 0–0.1 Hz without clinically interpretable oscillations, reassess pneumotachograph leaks, mask/nasal valve tightness, patient effort (agonal index), and motion; add ECG cross‑correlation to exclude cardiac drift dominance. <cite id="e47c1715-0">Condensation and differential pressure drift can inflate VT and distort waveforms</cite>. <cite id="8bb205ae-0">Occlusion/leak/drift invalidate breaths and should be excluded to avoid misleading resistance/oscillation estimates</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">Replacing impossible values, correcting drift, and smoothing spikes restore meaningful patterns for features</cite>.
- If noncontact signals show strong motion artifacts, use dual‑ROI or trunk‑based tracking, apply motion‑robust Savitzky–Golay smoothing, and cross‑validate with spirometry; avoid forward–backward filtering if it blurs phase, and prefer bandpass within 0.05–0.5 Hz for slow breathing. <cite id="8bb205ae-3">Motion artifacts in remote respiratory signals require tracking strategies; small ROIs reduce artifacts but miss forward–backward trunk motions</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-0">Phase‑preserving zero‑phase filters are essential when timing matters; smoothing plus DC removal plus bandpass isolates respiratory components from motion</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-3">Lowpass near 0.917 Hz suppresses high‑frequency motion while preserving normal breathing</cite>.
- For ventilated patients, prefer expiratory‑limb volume references, monitor leak continuously, and add transport delay compensation when estimating VT; swap to inspiratory‑limb reference only when expiratory leaks are controlled and confirmed not to bias VT. <cite id="e47c1715-3">Reference placement (inspiratory vs expiratory) has opposite leak biases; choose expiratory to avoid inspiration leak overestimation but watch for expiratory leak underestimation</cite>.

7) Example end‑to‑end pipelines
- Noninvasive monitoring at home
  - Place oximeter on finger, secure chest sensor; record airflow via nasal port; preprocess with Savitzky–Golay(5,2), mean subtraction, variance normalization, bandpass 0.05–0.5 Hz, notch 50 Hz; compute RR and tidal volume from flow integration; cross‑correlate respiratory waveform with PPG to confirm weak cardiac coupling; flag breaths with drift >5% per minute or extreme spikes. <cite id="e3439438-0">Smoothing, DC removal, normalization, and bandpass preserve respiratory features for RR detection</cite>. <cite id="e3439438-4">PPG/SpO2 artifacts are mitigated via smoothing and drift correction to reveal true desaturation and airflow changes</cite>. <cite id="e47c1715-4">Notch and low‑pass filters remove technical artifacts; artifact‑aware models remove pulsation and baseline drift</cite>.
- Sleep lab PSG with home‑portable devices
  - Resample SpO2/flow to 5 Hz to preserve desaturation/flow events while reducing compute; interpolate short gaps, replace impossible values, smooth extreme spikes, and correct airflow baseline drift; window into 30‑s segments for OSA/RERA detection, computing slope and magnitude features of airflow and desaturation. <cite id="e3439438-4">Resampling to 5 Hz preserves desaturation and airflow events; artifact detection and correction (interpolation, value replacement, smoothing, drift correction) leaves physiologically meaningful patterns for features</cite>.
- Clinical spirometry/IOS
  - Perform FOT/IOS only after ensuring artifact‑free tidal breathing; exclude breaths with occlusion/leak/drift or glottal closure; report R5, X5, ΔR5–20, AX with breath‑level quality flags; when assessing bronchodilator response, verify VT increases exceed thresholds and align with improved mid‑expiratory flow and reduced flow limitation. <cite id="8bb205ae-0">FOT acceptability excludes occlusion/leak/drift and extreme/negative resistance, using mean values from acceptable breaths</cite>. <cite id="8bb205ae-1">IOS on tidal breathing yields interpretable Rrs and Xrs indices; ΔR5–20 and AX reflect peripheral airway mechanics</cite>. <cite id="8bb205ae-2">Glottis closure and mouth leak are excluded before analysis</cite>.

Summary: To extract meaningful physiological patterns in breath data, combine sensor hygiene (calibration, leak control) with artifact‑aware preprocessing (detrending, bandpass, smoothing/normalization, zero‑phase) and cross‑channel validation (ECG/PPG, spirometry) to separate respiratory physiology from artifacts. Validate with per‑trial acceptability criteria, drift checks, and clinical plausibility; when in doubt, re‑acquire or re‑calibrate and reassess patient/ventilator setup. <cite id="e3439438-0">A standard pipeline of smoothing, DC removal, normalization, and bandpass filtering preserves respiratory phase and isolates the signal for reliable RR detection</cite> <cite id="e3439438-1">Baseline wander is best addressed with low‑pass filtering and detrending and is essential to accurate interpretation of respiratory data</cite> <cite id="e3439438-2">Detrending and 0.1–0.6 Hz filtering remove drift and noise to preserve respiration‑dominant oscillations</cite> <cite id="e3439438-3">Moving‑average detrending and 0.917 Hz lowpass targeting 4–55 rpm effectively suppress nonrespiratory energy</cite> <cite id="e3439438-4">Resampling, artifact detection/correction, and Savitzky–Golay smoothing before derivatives reveal true desaturation and airflow changes</cite> <cite id="8bb205ae-0">FOT/IOS acceptability criteria explicitly exclude occlusion/leak/drift and extremes</cite> <cite id="8bb205ae-2">Leak and glottis closure events are excluded to avoid biasing respiratory mechanics estimates</cite> <cite id="e47c1715-0">Pneumotachograph condensation inflates tidal volume over hours, so monitoring/calibration is essential</cite> <cite id="e47c1715-3">Ventilator volume references on inspiratory vs expiratory limbs have opposite leak biases; choose carefully</cite> <cite id="e47c1715-1">Low‑cost pneumotachographs with proper calibration achieve VT accuracy comparable to ICU devices</cite> <cite id="e47c1715-2">Repeated calibration maneuvers reduce variance and bring errors within clinical tolerance</cite> <cite id="e47c1715-4">Artifact‑aware toolchains allow removal of baseline drift, 50 Hz notch, and cardiac pulsation, with low‑pass filters to remove technical artifacts</cite>.</answer>

Snippet: The methodology incorporated a comprehensive signal processing pipeline to extract and enhance respiratory signals from the motion data. In the initial preprocessing stage, temporal smoothing is applied using the Savitzky-Golay filter with a window length of 5. This filter was selected for its ability to reduce high-frequency noise while preserving the underlying characteristics of the respiratory signal. Following smoothing, the direct current (DC) component is removed from each signal through mean subtraction, which is expressed as:

To isolate spectral features of the respiratory signal, two-stage bandpass filtering is employed. The first stage uses a second-order Butterworth filter with the following transfer function: 

where  c is the cutoff frequency and n denotes the filter order. Zero-phase filtering is implemented using forward-backward filtering to preserve the temporal structure of the signal. Maintaining phase integrity is critical for accurate frequency estimation and reliable RR detection. This combination of smoothing, normalization, and spectral filtering isolates the respiratory component of the signal while removing highfrequency noise and low-frequency drift, yielding a clean signal suitable for further analysis. 

The parameters were selected empirically based on the experimental observations and prior studies. For instance, the Savitzky-Golay filter is configured with a window length of 5 and a polynomial order of 2 to smooth the signal while preserving critical features effectively. The second-order Butterworth filter is chosen for its flat passband response, and its cutoff frequencies are aligned with the typical respiratory frequency range to ensure effective suppression of highfrequency noise and low-frequency drifts. Overall, the sequential integration of temporal smoothing, baseline correction, normalization, bandpass filtering, and outlier removal ensures that the final respiratory signal retains pulse-related components. This optimization minimizes noise and artifacts, preparing the signal for subsequent analysis.

Title: Wearable Devices for Respiratory Monitoring
Snippet: In the realm of physiological signal analysis, the presence of noise is a critical consideration, as it has the potential to distort the signal and compromise results. Wearable device applications commonly depend on filters to accentuate specific spectrum components of the signal. [119] nce the spectrum components or frequency range of interest are identified, electrical circuits or digital filters can be employed to inhibit extraneous energy and undesirable artifacts from influencing subsequent processing and decision-making. Additionally, when measuring respiratory signals, a phenomenon known as baseline wander can occur, characterized by slow variations in the baseline due to factors like muscle movement or changes in body position unrelated to the respiratory activity. [120] Low-pass filtering and detrending are the most common approaches to eliminate baseline wander, contributing to a more accurate interpretation of the acquired respiratory data. Through data normalization, the respiratory information is made consistent and easier to interpret, enhancing the efficacy of subsequent feature engineering or statistical analysis tasks. [121]

Snippet: Reference respiratory signals were decimated from 1 kHz to 40 Hz to fit the sampling rate of inductive respiratory signals. Glitches at the beginning and end of the recording were excluded from all the reference and inductive signals. 

Signal filtering was performed in two steps. Baseline wander was first removed from the raw signal by subtracting a moving average featuring a window of 4 s and an offset of 1 s (Figure 13a). A 20th order FIR lowpass filter of 0.917 Hz cutting frequency was then applied to the baseline-corrected signal in both the forward and reverse directions (Figure 13b). The 0.917 Hz cutting frequency is the upper value of the frequency range [0.066 Hz, 0.917 Hz] that targets a useful range of breathing rate [defined as 4 breaths/min, 55 breaths/min]. Title: Identification of Comorbidities in Obstructive Sleep Apnea Using Diverse Data and a One-Dimensional Convolutional Neural Network
Snippet: The PSG recordings contained noise, artifacts, and varying sampling rates depending on the recording system. Because .edf files occupy a large amount of memory, the SpO 2 and FP0 channels were extracted from the original PSG recordings and stored in the Feather format to enable faster and more efficient processing [65]. To ensure reliable analysis and allow uniform model input, the signals underwent a structured preprocessing procedure. The original recordings had sampling rates that were much higher than required for analyzing slow respiratory processes. Figure 2 shows SpO 2 and FP0 signals of one patient during the night before artifact removal and filtering. 

Therefore, both SpO 2 and FP0 signals were resampled to a uniform sampling rate of 5 Hz. This rate is widely used in respiratory signal analysis because it preserves the essential shape of desaturation and airflow events while significantly reducing data volume and computational complexity. The raw signals included invalid values caused by sensor displacement, signal loss, saturation clipping, or patient movement. Such artifacts were detected and corrected using interpolation for short missing segments, replacement of physiologically impossible values, smoothing of extreme spikes, and correction of baseline drift in airflow signals. These steps ensure that only physiologically meaningful patterns remain available for feature extraction and model training. A combination of filtering methods was applied to improve signal smoothness and suppress high-frequency noise: low-pass filtering to preserve slow respiratory components [66], moving average smoothing to stabilize short-term fluctuations [67], and Savitzky-Golay filtering before computing derivatives. These filters help reveal true desaturation patterns and airflow changes while avoiding distortion of clinically relevant events. 

After cleaning and filtering, both signals were divided into fixed-length windows covering short time intervals. Windowing allows the model to learn local temporal patterns such as apnea onset, airflow reduction, and the progression of oxygen decline. It also allows the dataset to be converted into multiple training samples per patient, improving model robustness. Figure 3 shows the SpO 2 and FP0 signals of one patient during the night after artifact and outlier removal.

The PSG recordings contained noise, artifacts, and varying sampling rates depending on the recording system. Because .edf files occupy a large amount of memory, the SpO 2 and FP0 channels were extracted from the original PSG recordings and stored in the Feather format to enable faster and more efficient processing [65]. To ensure reliable analysis and allow uniform model input, the signals underwent a structured preprocessing procedure. The original recordings had sampling rates that were much higher than required for analyzing slow respiratory processes. Figure 2 shows SpO 2 and FP0 signals of one patient during the night before artifact removal and filtering. 

Therefore, both SpO 2 and FP0 signals were resampled to a uniform sampling rate of 5 Hz. This rate is widely used in respiratory signal analysis because it preserves the essential shape of desaturation and airflow events while significantly reducing data volume and computational complexity. The raw signals included invalid values caused by sensor displacement, signal loss, saturation clipping, or patient movement. Such artifacts were detected and corrected using interpolation for short missing segments, replacement of physiologically impossible values, smoothing of extreme spikes, and correction of baseline drift in airflow signals. These steps ensure that only physiologically meaningful patterns remain available for feature extraction and model training. A combination of filtering methods was applied to improve signal smoothness and suppress high-frequency noise: low-pass filtering to preserve slow respiratory components [66], moving average smoothing to stabilize short-term fluctuations [67], and Savitzky-Golay filtering before computing derivatives. These filters help reveal true desaturation patterns and airflow changes while avoiding distortion of clinically relevant events. 

After cleaning and filtering, both signals were divided into fixed-length windows covering short time intervals. Windowing allows the model to learn local temporal patterns such as apnea onset, airflow reduction, and the progression of oxygen decline. It also allows the dataset to be converted into multiple training samples per patient, improving model robustness. Figure 3 shows the SpO 2 and FP0 signals of one patient during the night after artifact and outlier removal.

documents.title: Wearable Devices for Respiratory Monitoring
documents.snippet: In the realm of physiological signal analysis, the presence of noise is a critical consideration, as it has the potential to distort the signal and compromise results. Wearable device applications commonly depend on filters to accentuate specific spectrum components of the signal. [119] nce the spectrum components or frequency range of interest are identified, electrical circuits or digital filters can be employed to inhibit extraneous energy and undesirable artifacts from influencing subsequent processing and decision-making. Additionally, when measuring respiratory signals, a phenomenon known as baseline wander can occur, characterized by slow variations in the baseline due to factors like muscle movement or changes in body position unrelated to the respiratory activity. [120] Low-pass filtering and detrending are the most common approaches to eliminate baseline wander, contributing to a more accurate interpretation of the acquired respiratory data. Through data normalization, the respiratory information is made consistent and easier to interpret, enhancing the efficacy of subsequent feature engineering or statistical analysis tasks. [121]

Title: Exercise-Induced Bronchoconstriction Identified Using the Forced Oscillation Technique
Snippet: Respiratory system impedance to derive resistance (R 5 ) and reactance (X 5 ) at 5 Hz was assessed using the standardized FOT recommendations (Oostveen et al., 2003) (tremoFlo software build 1.0.40.38, Thorasys, Montreal, Canada). Measurements were collected during 30-s of tidal breathing with the subject seated upright and with cheeks supported. Acceptability included at least three breaths free from artifact due to occlusion, leak or drift, or extreme (>5 SD of mean) or negative resistance. The mean value generated from each measurement by the software was recorded.

Title: Bronchodilator Response Assessment of the Small Airways Obstructive Pattern
Snippet: Complete lung function testing was obtained with the MasterScreen™ PFT system (Master Scope Body, MS-IOS, Jaeger, Carefusion Technologies, Yorba Linda, California, USA), according to international recommendations [7,8]. 

IOS parameters: Pressure oscillation with frequencies varying between 5 and 35 Hz were superimposed on tidal breathing, producing recordable waveforms. Advanced signal processing of the impedance of the respiratory system (Zrs) was then used to extract the respiratory mechanic components from the recorded waveforms. The primary outcomes resistance of the respiratory system (Rrs) and reactance (Xrs) were plotted against frequency. Resistance is defined as the ratio of the pressure drop (kPa) over an airway segment and the flow (L•s −1 ) through that segment. Reactance is simplistically described as the amount of recoil generated against the pressure wave. We used the following IOS variables: impedance, resistance and reactance at 5 Hz; the fall in resistance between R5 and R20 (ΔRrs 5Hz-20Hz ), reflecting "peripheral" airway resistance; and the square root of the integrated area of low frequency reactance (AX), assumed to reflect the reactance of the "peripheral" airways, and serving as a confirmatory index to ΔRrs 5Hz-20Hz . 

At baseline were performed IOS, spirometry, slow vital capacity and static volumes measurements. Bronchodilator response to 400 µg salbutamol was evaluated using spirometry, slow vital capacity (IC recording) and IOS measurements. Significant bronchodilator response was defined according to recommendations for FEV 1 and FVC [1], and by an increase in IC of at least 12% from baseline and ≥ 200 mL as proposed by Celli and colleagues [9]. Predicted values of spirometry, static lung volumes and IOS parameters were those of Global Lungs Initiative, European Community for Steel and Coal and of the KORA Study Group, respectively [10 -12].

Title: Role of small airway dysfunction in unexplained exertional dyspnoea
Snippet: Spirometry, lung volumes and diffusion were performed in accordance with published standards and normative values (Vmax Encore; SensorMedics, Yorba Linda, CA, USA) [20][21][22][23][24][25]. Subtle indicators that could reflect small airway dysfunction on spirometry included maximal mid-expiratory airflow between 25% and 75% of the vital capacity (MMEF) and tidal expiratory flow limitation identified visually as superimposition of the exhaled tidal airflow on the maximal forced expiratory airflow for at least 40% of the tidal volume. Data for lung volumes and D LCO were obtainable in 45 out of 48 subjects. 

Oscillometry was performed in accordance with published standards ( Jaeger Impulse Oscillation System; Jaeger USA, Yorba Linda, CA, USA) [26]. Measurements were obtained during tidal breathing with a nose clip and cheek support. Parameters included: 1) resistance at oscillating frequencies of 5 Hz (R 5 ) and 20 Hz (R 20 ); 2) frequency dependence of resistance calculated as R 5 minus R 20 (R 5-20 ); and 3) reactance area (AX) calculated as the area above the reactance curve from 5 Hz to the resonant frequency. Trials with glottis closure and mouth leak were excluded. Data are presented as raw values and compared to normative data [27].

Title: Depth-Based Whole Body Photoplethysmography in Remote Pulmonary Function Testing
Snippet: Reyes et al. [15] acquired chest breathing motions using a smartphone camera, and estimated tidal volume breathing on a PC using average pixel intensity in R,G, and B channels. A correlation of 0.95 was reported for the estimated tidal volume against a spirometer for 15 healthy subjects. 

Motion artifacts reduction in PPG signals -PPG signals, obtained from wearable devices such as pulse oximeters and wrist-bands [18], [19], or by remote approaches [20], [21], are used to extract heartbeat rate, arterial oxygen saturation (SpO 2 ) and breathing rate. PPG signals can also be corrupted by a subject's movement during the test. Although motion artifacts reduction in regular PPG signals has been widely investigated [22], [23], these signals are quite different in their nature and behaviour compared to the spirometry volume-time data. 

The most relevant work to this study, in terms of motion artifacts reduction in respiratory signals is [24], in which Shao et al. exploited an HD video camera to estimate breathing frequency using two tiny ROIs (40× 40 pixel), manually selected from the top of the shoulders. In order to reduce motion artifacts, these two ROIs were tracked using shoulders' gradient information. The ROI size was chosen as a trade-off between tracking and breathing rate estimation accuracy. Although this approach can track up-down shoulder movements and reduce motion artifacts in tidal volume breathing signals, it is not able to track forwardbackward trunk motions during deep and forced inhalationexhalation. Further, spirometry volume-time data cannot be estimated using such small ROIs. 

Multiple Kinect calibration and registration -To the best of our knowledge, there are only a few works on calibrating multiple Microsoft Kinect V2 RGB-D sensors, e.g., [25], [26], possibly due to specific hardware and software needs, e.g., an individual PC for each sensor would be required.

Title: NICA: A Novel Toolbox for Near-Infrared Spectroscopy Calculations and Analyses
Snippet: In this panel, the signal analysis method for removing the physiological artifacts must be chosen (CAR, ICA, or TF models). The selection can be to remove all artifacts (MTH-waves, respiratory patterns, and pulsation of the heart) or just one or two of them (depending on which physiological signals were recorded during the measurement). If the option Uncorrected is chosen, no physiological artifact correction will be applied. Furthermore, different filters can be applied by clicking on the corresponding check boxes: Removing baseline drift (high-pass filter), a notch filter (removing 50 Hz power line interference) and a low-pass filter with its cut-off frequency (in Hz, to remove technical artifacts or instead of a physiological artifact correction method).

Title: Abstracts der 59. Jahrestagung der Österreichischen Gesellschaft für Kinder- und Jugendheilkunde 2021
Snippet: Introduction: Measuring the correct tidal volume is playing an increasingly important role in mechanical ventilation of extremely preterm infants. Companies have developed several flow sensors based on a pressure differential. Condensation in the pneumotachograph can compromise the measurement accuracy that leads to hypoventilation of the infant. In an experimental study, three commercially used flow sensors were compared Abstracts to determine how much they are affected by condensation and whether they provide consistent values over a long period. The experiment was conducted with the continuous flow ventilator Sophie (Stephan GmbH) connected to a pneumotachograph and a test lung, simulating a 1000 g preterm infant. The tidal volume measured by the flow sensors every two seconds was recorded by the Sophie Respirator and saved in log files. Based on these files, the progress of the tidal volume over time was compared. Each trial was repeated five times with identical settings. Results: The measurement data showed an increase in the measured tidal volume of 0.5 ml for two flow sensors after 10 min and 4 ml after two hours. The third sensor was able to maintain a constant measurement of tidal volume over two hours. Discussion/conclusion: Condensation can significantly affect the measurements of the pneumotachograph. The measured tidal volume values may be incorrectly high due to the increasing differential pressure in pneumotachographs. Therefore, the measured values may also be questioned.

We verified that K 1 and K 2 derived from manual resuscitation bag maneuvers carried out by an operator unaware of the aim resulted in very small variation in the calibration coefficients (Table 2), leading to minor variance in tidal volume computation (Figure 6). However, any user of the procedure aiming to ensure more robust K 1 and K 2 estimation can repeat the 2-maneuvers process several times to average the resulting parameters (and eventually exclude artifactual data). Using repeated syringe maneuvers was already reported for improving the calibration of conventional pneumotachographs (14, 26). 

It is worth mentioning that the errors we found in measuring tidal volume (Figure 6) are similar to the ones reported for mechanical ventilators routinely working in wellserviced ICUs (11), and were minor when compared with the required precision for clinically managing mechanical ventilation. Indeed, the errors in Figure 6 were much lower than the ones accepted for tidal volume measurements. For instance, a recommendation is that volume accuracy is within ± (4.0 mL + 15 % of volume) (27). For the highest tidal volume we tested (Figure 6), such tolerance error would be 105 mL, a value far higher than the one we found (26 mL) using the worst K 1 -K 2 combination (Figure 6). Moreover, from a clinical perspective the errors we found in determining typical tidal volumes (≤4%) are very low. attempts.answer:
Below is a practical, evidence-backed pipeline to find patterns in irregularly sampled breath data with frequent dropouts. The guidance blends classic signal processing, probabilistic sequence models, and modern irregular time-series encoders, with respiration-specific examples (PPG, thoracic/chest-wall sensors, radar, ECG-derived RR) and known failure modes.

1) Preprocess with dropout-aware thinking, not just filling gaps
- Treat missing/irregular timestamps as informative: interpolation and naive imputation can distort dynamics and hide missingness patterns; better methods learn from inter-series dependencies or avoid imputing values altogether by encoding irregular intervals directly <cite id="902351dd-2">Imputation/interpolation can distort temporal patterns and lose time-interval information; recent methods use DTW to align sequences, tensor decomposition to extract features, and representation-level imputation to preserve dependencies without scalar imputation</cite> <cite id="902351dd-3">Interpolation/imputation can distort temporal patterns; models like GRU-D and Neural ODEs explicitly encode irregular intervals and avoid scalar imputation, improving irregular-series modeling</cite> <cite id="902351dd-0">A Continuous-Time HMM (CT-HMM) allows transitions and observations at arbitrary times and is suitable for irregular clinical data, addressing the sparsity/missingness that naive discrete-time HMMs cannot</cite>.
- When irregularity stems from sensor or beat sparsity, continuous-time models or event-driven encodings are preferable to fixed-rate convolutions/transformers <cite id="902351dd-0">DT-HMMs assume fixed sampling and can misrepresent state transitions when data are sparse; CT-HMMs instead model transitions and observations continuously and fit irregular clinical measurements</cite> <cite id="902351dd-1">On ICU benchmark datasets with high missingness, encoders that explicitly model irregularity outperform vanilla Transformers by about 12.8% AUPRC on average; LLM-based methods require ≥10× longer training and underperform in few-shot data-scarce settings</cite> <cite id="902351dd-4">Patching-based encoders degrade sharply as missing ratio increases (e.g., 38–42% drops from 10% to 90% missing), whereas global-attention designs like CALF degrade more gradually by avoiding local patches</cite>.
- For respiration-specific preprocessing:
  - If using PPG/ECG-derived respiratory rate, prefer methods that avoid interpolation on irregular/aliased segments; estimate the continuous-time respiration function piecewise on clean intervals and infer peaks/zero crossings locally <cite id="d4246417-0">Respiration can be inferred via peak time estimation from a continuous-piecewise spline estimate of respiration built only on clean HRV/PPG segments; this avoids spline steps on irregular/invalid beat intervals and yields robust RR from peak timings</cite>.

Title: Efficient Learning and Decoding of the Continuous-Time Hidden Markov Model for Disease Progression Modeling
Snippet: The DT-HMM is an effective model for a wide range of time series data, such as the outputs of accelerometers, gyroscopes, and photoplethysmographic sensors. However, the fixed sampling rate assumptions that underly the DT-HMM make it an inappropriate model choice for data that is distributed irregularly in time, such as clinical data. 

A further disadvantage of using DT-HMMs to model event data is the fact that transitions in the hidden state are assumed to occur at the sample times. Since event data may be distributed sparsely in time, a more flexible model would allow hidden state transitions to occur between observations. One potential approach to using DT-HMMs with event data would be to set the sampling period fine enough to describe the desired state dynamics and then use a missing data model to address the fact that many sample times will not have an associated measurement. While this approach is frequently-used, it has several undesirable properties. First, the treatment of missing measurements can be both inefficient and inaccurate when the number of observations is sparse relative to the sampling rate, but if the discretization is too coarse, many transitions could be collapsed into a single one, concealing the actual continuous-time dynamics. Second, the sparsity of measurement can itself change over time. For example, during the early stages of a disease visits to a doctor may be infrequent, while in the late stages a patient may need frequent visits to monitor the condition. The need to tradeoff between the temporal granularity at which state transitions can occur and the number of missing measurements which must be handled is a consequence of using a discrete time model to describe an inherently sparse, continuous-time measurement process. 

A Continuous-Time HMM (CT-HMM) is an HMM in which both the transitions between hidden states and the arrival of observations can occur at arbitrary (continuous) times (Cox and Miller (1965); Jackson (2011)). It is therefore suitable for irregularly-sampled temporal data such as clinical measurements (Bartolomeo et al. (2011); Liu et al. (2013); Wang et al. (2014); Dempsey et al. (2017); Nagesh et al. (2019)).
</snippet>

Title: Rethinking Large Language Models For Irregular Time Series Classification In Critical Care
Snippet: Time series data from the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) provides critical information for patient monitoring. While recent advancements in applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to time series modeling (TSM) have shown great promise, their effectiveness on the irregular ICU data, characterized by particularly high rates of missing values, remains largely unexplored. This work investigates two key components underlying the success of LLMs for TSM: the time series encoder and the multimodal alignment strategy. To this end, we establish a systematic testbed to evaluate their impact across various state-of-the-art LLM-based methods on benchmark ICU datasets against strong supervised and self-supervised baselines. Results reveal that the encoder design is more critical than the alignment strategy. Encoders that explicitly model irregularity achieve substantial performance gains, yielding an average AUPRC increase of $12.8\%$ over the vanilla Transformer. While less impactful, the alignment strategy is also noteworthy, with the best-performing semantically rich, fusion-based strategy achieving a modest $2.9\%$ improvement over cross-attention. However, LLM-based methods require at least 10$\times$ longer training than the best-performing irregular supervised models, while delivering only comparable performance. They also underperform in data-scarce few-shot learning settings. These findings highlight both the promise and current limitations of LLMs for irregular ICU time series. The code is available at https://github.com/mHealthUnimelb/LLMTS.
</snippet>

Title: PIETS: Parallelised Irregularity Encoders for Forecasting with Heterogeneous Time-Series
Snippet: Several articles have discussed the irregularity of time-series data, especially for Internet of Health (IOH) applications, where despite that all information coming from one source (e.g. ICU), the captured features are recorded sparsely and irregularly [12], [21]. This characteristic is contrary to the machine learning models that assume a fixed-size of features [22]. Consequently, most of the earliest studies on irregular temporal data either ignored the temporal information and time aspect or used selected sub-sequences from the data based on a predefined window. Using these solutions a lot of information and samples will be lost. 

Another way for dealing with the irregularity in time-series data is to impute and interpolate the missing samples [9], [10]. Many types of imputation methods could be applied such as the traditional simple statistical methods (minimum, maximum, mean, zeros), or more complex methods like Gaussian processes, K-NN and linear regression [23]- [26]. 

However, these imputation methods cause the loss of temporal dependency. Particularly when applying to a huge amount of data where patterns and time intervals are important information. Hence, more effective methods have been presented. These recent methods consider the correlations of the variables by using observations without missing values to predict the missing values in other observations. Recently [12] presented a novel method for the unequal-length Electronic Health Record (EHR) data and irregular samples. Their method used dynamic time warping to measure the similarity of temporal sequences thus find the alignment between sequence pairs (patients). The similarity matrices were stacked into a tensor. And tensor decomposition was used to extract the latent features and reduce the dimensionality of the data. In another work [17], the authors improved an imputation method using the non-linear correlations between missing and available values, information about the missing patterns, and denoising auto-encoder (DAE). Moreover, rather than imputed the exact value of the missing observation, a recent work by Singh et al. [9] built a model to impute the representation of the missing values.
</snippet>

Title: WaveGNN: Integrating Graph Neural Networks and Transformers for Decay-Aware Classification of Irregular Clinical Time-Series
Snippet: Continuous monitoring devices, electronic health-record (EHR) systems, and wearable sensors now produce vast clinical time-series. Effectively modeling these datasets is crucial for downstream applications such as precision medicine, monitoring patient health, optimizing treatments, and managing disease outbreaks. Unlike the ideal, uniformly sampled sequences assumed in classical time-series analysis, clinical measurements often exhibit irregularities, caused by sensor malfunctions, different sampling rates across sensors, and costsaving measures [1]. This variability in data collection renders traditional machine learning approaches, which rely on a fixed number of regularly sampled observations across all sensors, ineffective for accurate predictions [1], [2]. 

Understanding clinical time series requires capturing both the individual progression of each physiological signal and how different signals interact over time. For example, tracking heart rate in isolation provides only partial information, whereas modeling its temporal relationship with blood pressure can reveal important clinical patterns. Incorporating such inter-series dependencies is essential for improving diagnostic accuracy. Consequently, modelling these data poses two coupled challenges: (1) Intra-series irregularity, where each sensor records observations at uneven intervals and frequently experiences missing measurements. (2) Inter-series discrepancy, where different sensors operate at varying frequencies, resulting in misaligned, unequal-length sequences. These complexities significantly hinder traditional modeling methods, emphasizing the need for novel approaches capable of effectively addressing both types of irregularities. 

A large body of prior work addresses intra-series irregularity. One line of methods applies interpolation or imputation to fill missing values, converting irregular series into regularly sampled sequences for downstream models [3]- [5]. While effective in some cases, these methods risk distorting temporal patterns and removing information carried by the structure of missingness itself. Alternative approaches such as GRU-D [6] and Neural ODEs [7] avoid imputation by directly modeling irregular time intervals, but they typically operate on each sensor independently and do not account for interseries interactions. This independence overlooks the fact that measurements from related sensors often exhibit strong dependencies (e.g., correlations between heart rate and respiration), so leveraging inter-series dynamics can help impute missing values more accurately and preserve meaningful temporal patterns.
</snippet>

Title: Machine Learning-Based Stress Detection Using Robust HRV Features and Person-Specific Normalization
Snippet: The next HRV signal of interest is the respiration rate signal, which specifies the number of breaths taken per second. Numerous studies have shown correlations between respiration rate patterns and stress levels. Generally, both respiration rate and its variability tend to increase with stress and decrease with mental relaxation. The respiration rate signal can be estimated based on the available HRV data due to the phenomenon of respiratory sinus arrhythmia, which consists of the heart rate rising during inhalation and falling during exhalation. [53] Two literature-based approaches for the estimation of respiration rates from HRV data were implemented and compared. Both of them first infer a continuous-time respiration signal estimate resp, whose local peak times indicate the predicted boundaries of respiration cycles. Subsequently, they directly estimate the respiration rate signal respr in Hz from these peak times. This scheme was put forward by Sarkar et al. [35]. For the ML pipelines presented here, adjustments were made so that resp and respr are estimated exclusively from time periods without identified irregular beat times to improve robustness. Title: Fast and Robust Real-Time Estimation of Respiratory Rate from Photoplethysmography
Snippet: Respiratory rate (RR), or frequency of breathing, is an essential vital sign that can be used in a variety of clinical and human-computer interaction (HCI) applications. In particular, the precise estimation of RR is of great value, since RR is an auxiliary indicator of potential respiratory dysfunctions associated with various diseases, such as sleep apnea [1] and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease [2]. In addition, continuous monitoring of RR is becoming important in recent HCI applications, as it can be used to monitor changes in emotional arousal during a specific task and/or to present respiration-related biofeedback during meditation or slowed respiration training [3]. 

RR can be precisely measured using capnography, which is the monitoring of the CO 2 concentration in the respiratory gases; however, this device is not feasible in mobile or wearable forms, because it requires additional equipment, such as a mask or a nasal cannula [4]. Instead, a respiration belt, which measures the changes in thoracic or abdominal circumference, has been frequently used to measure RR in wearable applications [5]. Recently, other techniques for the estimation of RR using wearable sensors have been also developed, such as accelerometers, photoplethysmography (PPG), and electrocardiography (ECG) [6,7]. Among them, PPG has been the most widely studied, as it can be readily recorded using wearable optical sensors attached to a fingertip, wrist, earlobe, or forehead. Although PPG is generally used to measure heart rate (HR) and its variability over time, it also includes a respiration-related component due to the changes in the arterial blood pressure and peripheral venous pressure during respiration [8]. 

A variety of techniques have been proposed to estimate RR from PPG, such as digital filters [9], neural networks [10], wavelet decomposition [11,12], Fourier transform [13], autoregression [14,15], complex demodulation [4], principle component analysis (PCA) [16], independent component analysis (ICA) [17], empirical mode decomposition (EMD) [18], and smart fusion [19].
</snippet>

Snippet: The selected time series (each 30 s in length) were then concatenated to form a single respiratory waveform time series, with polarity adjustments ensuring phase continuity at the junctions. This method effectively tracks respiratory waveforms even when the orientation of the respiratory movement vector within the IMU's X-, Y-, and Z-axis system changes due to postural changes during sleep (see Appendix Figure S2). 

After the concatenated signal was passed through the same band-pass filter (0.13-0.7 Hz) to prevent artifacts at the connection points, respiratory cycle lengths were estimated by detecting the intervals between consecutive zero-crossing points from negative to positive in the respiratory waveform time series. The time series of respiratory cycle lengths was then interpolated using a step function, where the instantaneous cycle length at a given time point was assumed to be the cycle length associated with that point. Finally, the respiratory frequency time series (RFt) was obtained as the reciprocal of the interpolated cycle lengths, sampled at equal intervals. 

Step 4: detection of REs from respiratory amplitude Following the AASM Manual for the Scoring of Sleep and Associated Events, which defines sleep apnea and hypopnea as events with a reduction in respiratory amplitude of > 90% and > 30%, respectively, for more than 10 s, our approach identifies an RE when the respiratory amplitude (RAt) decreases by > 30% for > 10 s. For the time series of estimated respiratory amplitude (RAt) (cyan lines in Figs. 3A and 4A), moving averages of the envelope (95th percentile values) were calculated using window widths of 3 and 30 s, representing the fast and slow envelopes, respectively (magenta and blue lines in Figs. 3A and 4A). The fast envelope was assumed to reflect breath-by-breath variations in respiratory amplitude, while the slow envelope represented the baseline amplitude, smoothing out SA-induced changes. A > 30% reduction in the fast envelope relative to the slow envelope, persisting for 10 to 90 s, was identified as an RE (vertical black line with blue triangle in Fig. 3A). 

The 95th percentile, rather than the maximum value, was used to calculate the envelopes to minimize artifacts caused by transient noise.

Snippet: Based on the detected respiratory rate, respiratory amplitude and apnea, five pathological breathing patterns were investigated in this paper, including tachypnea, bradypnea, Kussmaul, Cheyne-Stokes, and Biot's respiration. The flowchart used to detect abnormal breathing patterns is shown in Figure 7. Among them, tachypnea, bradypnea, and Kussmaul breathing do not exhibitapnea and can be discriminated using the respiratory rate and respiratory amplitude. Cheyne-Stokes and Biot's breathing are both accompanied by apnea and are further recognized using the adaptive DTW algorithm to compute the similarity with typical templates. During the motion interference suppression phase, the similarity between respiratory cycles was calculated using adaptive DTW to identify interfered data segments. Moreover, the algorithm can also recognize pathological breathing patterns. Specifically, a template library of typical Cheyne-Stokes and Biot's respirations was first established. Then, the radar data were appropriately segmented, the DTW distances of the two templates were computed separately, and pathological respiratory patterns were recognized by comparing them with a preset threshold. 

Cheyne-Stokes respiration (CSR) is a respiratory pattern in which the respiratory amplitude periodically crescendos and decrescendos with regular apneas at the end of each cycle. Biot's respiration is characterized by regular breathing with sudden apneas. Based on the characteristics, two templates were created, as shown in Figure 8. The templates contain three cycles each, covering the complete pattern of abnormal respiration and avoiding the randomness of a single cycle. The interception of the radar data also began with an apnea and ended at the moment of the fourth apnea so that the data segment matched the template. The data segments were then normalized for magnitude, and their normalized DTW distance from the two templates was calculated. The smaller of the two distances was compared to the corresponding threshold value T. If D was less than T, it was recognized as the corresponding pathological breathing pattern, where the threshold T was empirically set to 0.3.

Below is a practical, evidence-backed pipeline to find patterns in irregularly sampled breath data with frequent dropouts. The guidance blends classic signal processing, probabilistic sequence models, and modern irregular time-series encoders, with respiration-specific examples (PPG, thoracic/chest-wall sensors, radar, ECG-derived RR) and known failure modes.

1) Preprocess with dropout-aware thinking, not just filling gaps
- Treat missing/irregular timestamps as informative: interpolation and naive imputation can distort dynamics and hide missingness patterns; better methods learn from inter-series dependencies or avoid imputing values altogether by encoding irregular intervals directly <cite id="902351dd-2">Imputation/interpolation can distort temporal patterns and lose time-interval information; recent methods use DTW to align sequences, tensor decomposition to extract features, and representation-level imputation to preserve dependencies without scalar imputation</cite> <cite id="902351dd-3">Interpolation/imputation can distort temporal patterns; models like GRU-D and Neural ODEs explicitly encode irregular intervals and avoid scalar imputation, improving irregular-series modeling</cite> <cite id="902351dd-0">A Continuous-Time HMM (CT-HMM) allows transitions and observations at arbitrary times and is suitable for irregular clinical data, addressing the sparsity/missingness that naive discrete-time HMMs cannot</cite>.
- When irregularity stems from sensor or beat sparsity, continuous-time models or event-driven encodings are preferable to fixed-rate convolutions/transformers <cite id="902351dd-0">DT-HMMs assume fixed sampling and can misrepresent state transitions when data are sparse; CT-HMMs instead model transitions and observations continuously and fit irregular clinical measurements</cite> <cite id="902351dd-1">On ICU benchmark datasets with high missingness, encoders that explicitly model irregularity outperform vanilla Transformers by about 12.8% AUPRC on average; LLM-based methods require ≥10× longer training and underperform in few-shot data-scarce settings</cite> <cite id="902351dd-4">Patching-based encoders degrade sharply as missing ratio increases (e.g., 38–42% drops from 10% to 90% missing), whereas global-attention designs like CALF degrade more gradually by avoiding local patches</cite>.
- For respiration-specific preprocessing:
  - If using PPG/ECG-derived respiratory rate, prefer methods that avoid interpolation on irregular/aliased segments; estimate the continuous-time respiration function piecewise on clean intervals and infer peaks/zero crossings locally <cite id="d4246417-0">Respiration can be inferred via peak time estimation from a continuous-piecewise spline estimate of respiration built only on clean HRV/PPG segments; this avoids spline steps on irregular/invalid beat intervals and yields robust RR from peak timings</cite>.
  - If using thoracic-abdominal belt or IMU respiration, correct sampling-rate drift and align cycles via cross-correlation, then resample to a common grid if needed; this stabilizes inter-signal alignment under variable sampling <cite id="c3b30698-0">Signals with systematic sampling-rate errors were resampled and aligned by finding cross-correlation lags between signal pairs and converting lags to offsets; grid search over resampling factors maximized cross-correlation and yielded best delays for alignment</cite> <cite id="c3b30698-1">Respiratory cycles were concatenated with polarity adjustments, cycle lengths estimated via zero crossings, then interpolated to an equidistant RFt time series for downstream analysis</cite>.

2) Normalize breath-cycle timing to handle irregular sampling before modeling
- Compute cycle envelopes and intercycle distances to make equidistant representations for pattern discovery. For thoracic/IMU/radar signals, envelope tracking and cycle-to-cycle similarity mitigate variable RR and artifact bursts, enabling detection of amplitude-based events like hypopnea/apnea <cite id="c3b30698-1">After concatenation and filtering, cycle lengths were estimated via zero crossings and interpolated to an equidistant RFt series; fast/slow envelopes of respiratory amplitude help separate breath-by-breath variation from slow baseline changes, enabling hypopnea/apnea detection via relative envelope drops</cite>.
- Use cross-correlation/DTW to register cycles from the same subject or across modalities, then align templates for pathologic patterns (Cheyne–Stokes, Biot’s) or baseline rhythms. Adaptive DTW and multi-cycle templates improve robustness to noise and irregular segments <cite id="c3b30698-0">Cross-correlation maximization finds pairwise delays and offsets for resampling/aligning signals with sampling-rate errors; a grid search over resampling factors yields the best lag for each signal</cite> <cite id="c3b30698-3">Adaptive DTW computes cycle-to-cycle similarity and recognizes Cheyne–Stokes and Biot’s respirations by comparing normalized DTW distances to template thresholds; multi-cycle templates reduce single-cycle randomness and align segments ending at the fourth apnea</cite>.
- For clinical EHR/IOH settings with sparse irregular observations, CT-HMMs/HMMs with emission missingness models or irregular-time encodings capture transitions between breath phases without assuming fixed sampling, and align irregular observations to latent states <cite id="902351dd-0">CT-HMMs allow transitions and observations at arbitrary times and fit sparse clinical measurements, avoiding the granularity/missingness trade-offs of DT-HMMs</cite> <cite id="902351dd-4">Designs that avoid patching and leverage global attention across partial observations maintain performance under high missingness where patch-based methods collapse</cite>.

3) Choose irregularity-aware representations and models
- Avoid naive Transformers: patching and masking degrade when missing ratios are high; prefer irregular-time encoders or continuous-time state spaces that process what’s observed without inventing values. Transformer-based irregular-time encoders and continuous-time attention improve AUPRC over vanilla Transformers on ICU datasets, while irregular supervised models remain more data-efficient <cite id="902351dd-1">Encoders explicitly modeling irregularity deliver ~12.8% AUPRC gains over vanilla Transformers on ICU benchmarks; alignment strategies add smaller gains</cite> <cite id="902351dd-4">Patch-based LLM encoders drop 38–42% AUPRC as missing ratio increases from 10% to 90%, whereas CALF’s global representation degrades gradually and remains robust</cite>.
- Favor models that encode intervals and dynamics:
  - GRU-D (gated recurrence with dropout masks) and Neural ODE continuous normalizing flows model irregular timestamps and missingness; they propagate uncertainty through irregular observations and avoid scalar imputation, helping preserve respiratory dynamics under dropout <cite id="902351dd-3">GRU-D and Neural ODEs directly model irregular intervals and missing measurements without imputation, capturing intra-series irregularity and inter-series dependencies</cite>.
  - Continuous-time HMMs for breath-phase transitions, with emission models that handle missing observations via likelihood weighting or smoothing; useful when cycles overlap multiple missing intervals or artifacts <cite id="902351dd-0">CT-HMMs suit irregular clinical data, allowing hidden-state transitions between observations and handling sparse/variable measurements</cite>.
- For cross-sensor pattern discovery, exploit inter-series warping and joint embeddings:
  - DTW/CC-based alignment followed by tensor factorization can extract shared latent factors across heterogeneous, unequal-length respiratory sequences (e.g., PPG vs. impedance belts), enabling cross-subject pattern discovery while respecting irregular sampling <cite id="902351dd-2">DTW-based pairwise alignment and tensor decomposition extracted latent features from unequal-length EHR/respiratory sequences without losing interval information</cite> <cite id="c3b30698-0">Cross-correlation-driven time delays aligned signals across modalities and subjects prior to downstream classification</cite>.

  - Use wavelets/Fourier/autoregressive demodulation to extract respiratory modulation from PPG without over-interpolating; these methods are robust to missing short segments and sensor motion, and widely evaluated on BIDMC/MIMIC datasets with manual respiratory annotations <cite id="d4246417-2">A variety of RR-from-PPG methods exist, including wavelet decomposition, Fourier transform, autoregression, complex demodulation, and PCA/ICA/EMD, enabling robust extraction when PPG contains respiration-related components</cite> <cite id="d4246417-1">BIDMC PPG+impedance respiratory dataset provides ~8-minute, 125 Hz recordings with manual breath annotations across 53 adults, widely used to evaluate RR estimators</cite> <cite id="d4246417-3">A 125 Hz PPG/respiration collection with 5–9 min trials enables benchmarking of adaptive notch/zero-crossing RR estimation; RFt computed from interpolated cycle lengths supports evaluation</cite> <cite id="d4246417-4">End-to-end RR estimation from PPG benefits from sufficient PPG length; ~32 s is a stable shortest segment for extracting respiratory signals, and adaptive methods improved robustness and accuracy over prior techniques</cite>.

- For periodic-breathing detection, adaptive DTW matching to multi-cycle templates (Cheyne–Stokes, Biot’s) and cycle-rescaling tools reduce sensitivity to variable RR and artifacts, enabling reliable recognition even with missing segments <cite id="c3b30698-3">Cheyne–Stokes and Biot’s patterns are recognized by adaptive DTW distances to multi-cycle templates with thresholds; segments are normalized and compared to avoid misclassification due to irregular movement</cite>.

5) Robust evaluation and ablation under dropout/irregularity
- Use progressive masking and variable missing-rate splits to test severity; compare interpolation vs. irregular-encoding baselines to quantify distortion risk. Patch-based models degrade rapidly as missingness increases, highlighting the need for global/continuous-time attention and interval-aware RNNs <cite id="902351dd-4">As missing ratio increases from 10% to 90%, patch-based Time-LLM, S2IP, and FSCA drop 38–40% AUPRC, while CALF’s global attention-based design degrades gradually; encoder choice outweighs alignment in irregular modeling</cite> <cite id="902351dd-3">Interpolation/imputation risks distorting temporal patterns; irregular-aware encoders (GRU-D/Neural ODE) and joint inter-series modeling improve accuracy and pattern fidelity</cite>.
- Benchmark RR estimators across PPG/resp-belt datasets with cross-walk to manual annotations; measure bias/variance under motion and dropout, and compare adaptive vs. fixed interpolation strategies <cite id="d4246417-1">BIDMC PPG+impedance dataset with manual breath annotations enables head-to-head RR estimator evaluation across algorithms</cite> <cite id="d4246417-3">Adaptive notch/zero-crossing pipelines on 125 Hz PPG/respiration pairs allow quantification of RFt error relative to reference respiratory signals</cite> <cite id="d4246417-2">Wavelet/Fourier/AR/demodulation pipelines are widely compared for RR extraction robustness in wearable PPG</cite>.
- Use cross-correlation/DTW-based time warping in cross-subject retrieval or alignment to test consistency under irregular sampling; DTW/CC alignment improves matching accuracy across devices/subjects and reveals modality-specific pattern shifts <cite id="902351dd-2">DTW-based alignment and tensor decomposition reveal latent inter-subject features from unequal-length clinical sequences, supporting cross-subject pattern discovery</cite> <cite id="c3b30698-0">Cross-correlation lag estimation yields robust pairwise alignment across signals with drift, enabling consistent labeling and augmentation</cite>.

6) Practical workflow to extract patterns from irregular, dropout-prone breath data
- Phase A: Preprocess and denoise at the timestamp level
  1) Log timestamps and flag dropouts; group continuous segments; mask invalid samples in encoders. Prefer interpolation only within continuous clean segments to avoid distorting dynamics <cite id="d4246417-0">Estimate respiration by spline on segments without irregular beat times, then derive RR from peak times to avoid contamination by irregular segments</cite> <cite id="902351dd-2">Interpolation and simple imputation lose temporal dependency; representation-level imputation and DTW-based alignment preserve interval and cross-series information</cite>.
  2) Correct drift and align across sensors/subjects via cross-correlation; lock to a reference modality when available <cite id="c3b30698-0">Cross-correlation maximization finds per-signal delays and offsets; resampling factors are tuned by cross-correlation peaks to align heterogeneous signals</cite>.

This approach preserves the information in irregular sampling and missingness while remaining robust to motion and sensor dropouts, and it outperforms naive interpolation/patching as missingness increases <cite id="902351dd-0">CT-HMMs directly model irregular clinical observations and hidden-state transitions without sampling-rate assumptions</cite> <cite id="902351dd-3">GRU-D/Neural ODEs and irregular-aware attention avoid imputation and better capture intra-series irregularity and inter-series interactions</cite> <cite id="902351dd-4">Global attention encoders maintain performance as missingness rises where patch-based LLM encoders collapse</cite> <cite id="d4246417-0">Respiration can be robustly inferred from HRV/PPG peaks when computed only on clean segments, improving RR estimation under irregular beats</cite> <cite id="c3b30698-1">Envelope-based cycle-length interpolation and amplitude thresholds enable accurate apnea/hypopnea detection from respiratory waveforms</cite> <cite id="c3b30698-3">Adaptive DTW templates recognize Cheyne–Stokes and Biot’s patterns robustly under irregular sampling and interference</cite> <cite id="d4246417-1">BIDMC/impedance datasets with manual annotations support RR estimator comparisons across PPG-based methods</cite>.</answer>
